When fermionic atoms reach ultra-low temperatures, they tend to occupy the ground state, leading to the formation of Bose-Einstein condensate behavior governed by Pauli exclusion. In contrast, atoms subject to strong interaction behaviors, such as those described by Fermi-Hubbard models, exhibit antiferromagnetic ordering at low temperatures. While both systems display "fermionic pairing"—where particles spontaneously organize into correlated pairs—their fundamental physical mechanisms diverge significantly. This research investigates ultracold fermionic atoms in the context of Fermi-Hubbard physics, highlighting the intricate parallels and distinctions between these coupled spin systems and very different superfluids.

Real-time computation of real-time varying matrices and their inverses is vital to many applications in control engineering, computer vision, and robotics. This paper introduces a new Zeroing Neural Network (ZNN) designed to address this need. The proposed ZNN model generates a time-evolving solution for the inverse of a real-time square matrix $A$ by integrating the Levenberg-Marquardt method with a time-varying coefficient. Unlike previous approaches that rely on the assumption of a small relaxation time to achieve high precision, the proposed network demonstrates the capability to compute exact inverses without this constraint. Extensive simulations were conducted to evaluate its performance under both constant and changing conditions. The experimental results highlight the Zero Neural Network's rapid convergence, robustness against noise, and strong real-time capabilities.

Visual systems in vertebrates feature parallel "on" and "off" pathways derived from retinal ganglion cells, a structure responsible for stable edge detection despite changing lighting conditions. We present a computational model of these pathways utilizing deep learning to address this issue. Our approach consists of a dual-stream convolutional network where paired filters within each stream learn to respond to specific local contrast states. We employed adversarial learning to have a subsequent generator, sensitive to these features, reconstruct an image grounded in current illumination but free from specific edges. Using the CIFAR10 dataset, we successfully generated a result where a recognizable face emerges from a clean background after being superimposed with patterns that triggered the dual-stream contrast mechanisms. We believe these findings offer a fresh perspective on visual processing mechanisms in vertebrates.

We are currently investigating the optimization of mirror configurations for wide-field X-ray telescopes that cover the 0.3 to 2.0 keV spectrum. The goal involves finding a set of spherical or deformed conical surfaces to maximize the telescope's effective area within specified angular resolution and field-of-view constraints. Because the design criteria are defined by inequality conditions, they translate into boundary conditions for our optimization model. We are employing a sequential quadratic programming (SQP) algorithm, which transforms each iteration into a quadratic optimization problem. In the first phase, we are solving these sub-problems using reduced or two-dimensional forms of the optical equations. Consequently, we have successfully identified four superior mirror configurations utilizing arrays of four polished elliptical cones, each segmented into four zones, achieving an effective area of 580 cm². These designs maintain a full width at half-maximum (FWHM) angular resolution of 5.2 arcminutes and cover a field of view (FOV) extending to 16.8 arcminutes.

Bloch's theorem forms the cornerstone of standard solid-state theory, serving as the fundamental basis for numerous computational methods essential to investigating quantum materials. However, not all substances adhere to this principle, prompting the need to identify more generalized forms that encompass broader classes of quantum systems. In this work, we present scalar Bloch-like theorems tailored for quantum materials lacking translational symmetry, maintaining consistency with standard Bloch theory where translational symmetry exists. These theorems serve as a critical foundation for developing generalized versions of well-established solid-state concepts for materials where translational symmetry is absent.

This paper presents a fresh investigation into steganography, focusing on developing a secure, confidential, and robust system using the Language model and the "write 1" algorithm with finite state Markov models. While our novel system leverages Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks for its predictive model, distinguishing it from prior research, experimental validation was conducted on English and the Chinese driving theory test. Our results indicate that the LSTM-based language model effectively embeds data in a substantially larger proportion of text compared to previous techniques. Furthermore, our system surpasses existing methods regarding both secrecy and capacity, demonstrating adaptability for various languages and other predictive models that rely on language-specific training data.

Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge for global transmission system operators (TSOs), serving as the foundation for transmission system use and expansion planning. Constraint screening is particularly important in this context, as it can drastically reduce computational costs and shorten solution times. This paper introduces a novel screening method for both nodal and bus-coupled UC models that leverages the theoretical bounds of dual variables to enhance node-coupled terms derived from power flow equations. By extracting specific information from the resulting relaxed network solutions to refine these bounds, the approach can be applied iteratively. Testing on the UCTE LMP 130-bus model demonstrates significant reductions in commitment variables, transmission use rights, and overall solution duration.

We examined the influence of hydrostatic pressure on the magnetic ordering temperature ($T_N$) of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ by applying X-ray diffraction and inelastic neutron scattering techniques coupled with density functional theory. Contrasting results with those observed in the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ polymorphs, $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO3 exhibits a significant rise in $T_N$ under pressure. This counterintuitive behavior stems from the suppression of the nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic interaction ($J_{nn}$) which outweighs the stronger enhancement provided to nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic interactions ($J_{nnn}$). Consequently, the pressure-tunability of $T_N$ in this material offers a novel experimental avenue for resolving long-standing disputes regarding its magnetism.

Synthetic Control (SC) methods are renowned for producing robust causal inferences regarding policy impacts, yet they typically rely on linear combinations of covariates. This approach, known as SC-linear, often fails to fully capture the nuanced dynamics of data. Building on recent advances in multiplicative SC methods, however, paves a path for synthetic construction that accommodates both linear and multiplicative interactions. Our study proposes a novel extension termed multiplicative SC-covariance, or multiplicative SC-covariance (mSC-covariance), adapting traditional cross-covariance relationships to include non-linear interactions. Specifically, we develop a method for estimating the multiplicative SC-covariance, enabling the generation of synthsctic units capable of capturing non-linear covariate effects at the target entity. To demonstrate its efficacy, theoretical properties such as the derivation of the best estimator are established. Empirical validation using U.S. state-level mortality rates following the September 11, 2001, attacks reveals that our proposed approach not only outperforms traditional SC-covariance approaches but also yields superior forecasts.

Graphs serve as a powerful tool for modeling structured data, yet the vast array of possible graphs renders comprehensive analysis challenging. This study introduces an unsupervised clustering method that leverages the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance, a metric designed to quantify graph dissimilarities and facilitate detailed examination. We address the critical challenge of accelerating GW distance computation for large-scale datasets by introducing a novel, accelerated approximation method based on a specialized disintegration of the GW distance tailored for efficient implementation. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly reduces computational time with minimal impact on clustering accuracy, outperforming several current graph embedding techniques in both clustering performance and robustness.

This study investigates the interaction between two electron bunches formed in sequence: one driven by an evolving plasma bubble behind an intense laser pulse within a plasma channel. The preceding electron bunch, accelerated to ultra-relativistic velocities, traverses the plasma channel and impinges upon the subsequent bubble. During this encounter, energy is transferred to the later-accelerated electrons, causing a modification in the later bubble's morphology. We examine how parameters such as the position and dimensions of the plasma channel, alongside the properties of the initial electron burst, affect this interaction. Beam characteristics including density, longitudinal position, and energy spectrum are analyzed. Observations reveal that the energy gain by electrons within the bubble fluctuates significantly due to instability induced by the collision with the prior bunch. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for investigating plasma-based mechanisms designed to merge or separate particle beams.

Using natural platinum and a high-purity germanium detector, researchers have investigated neutrinoless double-beta decay across several decay channels. This study establishes new limits at the 90% confidence level for decay outcomes involving beta-plus emission, electron capture, excited-state double-beta decay, and single or double neutron emission. Specific limits reported are: $1.8\times 10^{21}$ years for $\beta\beta^0$ in $^{194}$Pt, $< 1.2\times 10^{21}$ years for $\beta\beta^0$ in $^{196}$Pt to the $^{196}$Pb excited state, $< 1.2\times 10^{21}$ years for $\beta\beta^0$ in $^{198}$Pt to the $^{198}$Pd excited state, and $< 1.2\times 10^{21}$ years for $\beta\beta^0$ in $^{192,194,196}$Pt to the corresponding ground states. No prior measurements existed for the former two cases. Consequently, no statistically significant excess events were detected in any of the examined modes.

The axial-anomaly equation in QCD introduces a total derivative into the flavor-singlet axial-vector current, $J_5^\mu$. This paper demonstrates that the specific form taken by the chiral anomaly in the equation—specifically the topological term $Q^\mu$—is constrained by consistency with the self-duality properties and the specific boundary conditions of the gluon field. The field's topological charge serves as the summary metric for the density of $Q^\mu$. Our analysis shows that the gluon field's boundary conditions introduce an arbitrary constant $c$ within the expression of $Q^\mu$. We analyze this resulting family of currents and demonstrate that while an anomaly-free theory of gravity couples most elegantly to the current where $c=0$, with the exception of this singular instance, all other variations in the anomaly can be recognized as physical.

This paper introduces a new single-image super-resolution framework designed for color-and-mono dual-camera systems, leveraging their complementary strengths: the color camera for rich hue information and the mono camera for high resolution. The core innovation is a shared encoder-based neural architecture that processes both images through an identical encoder using zero-padding to downsample, followed by individual decoders for super-resolution using bilinear upscaling. After the decoders generate images alongside residual features at high rates, the system computes a feature correlation matrix to eliminate redundancy before outputting the final result in a fully end-to-end, training-independent manner. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that this fully automatic method achieves performance comparable to, or exceeding, that of existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Public transport is essential for achieving low-carbon travel; however, road transportation accounts for more than 70% of Europe's public transport volume, with bus usage comprising the vast majority and electric vehicles representing less than one percent. Consequently, implementing electric buses is a critical step toward reducing emissions. The primary obstacle to this transition is that the total number of bus depots and charging infrastructure is insufficient to accommodate all vehicles. Therefore, depots must be shared. This paper presents an approach for determining the optimal bus parking assignments to minimize energy consumption while ensuring punctuality on routes. We formulate this as an integer linear program (ILP) and solve it through a dual heuristic capable of simultaneously scheduling vehicles and allocating depots. Our testing using real-world datasets demonstrates that our proposed method is highly effective, yielding significant benefits from sharing depot resources.

Few-shot learning is an emerging field dedicated to developing models capable of generalizing to new classes with minimal labeled data. The standard challenge involves identifying categories from a small set of exemplars, typically addressed by generating pseudo-labels for unlabeled samples using multiple weak classifiers trained independently on the few available shots in multiple ensemble methods. This approach relies on these weak classifiers having sufficient capacity to yield meaningful diversity required for strong final performance. However, few text-based reports address whether these weak classifiers are actually capable of generating the necessary variety among the few input shots. We demonstrate empirically—through rigorous experiments on multiple standard datasets—that current weak classifier architectures fail to produce adequate diversity. Consequently, we identify a lack of variety as the root cause of limited improvement and introduce ShotPruner, a novel algorithm that enhances diversity by pruning redundant samples and reintroducing new ones multiple times until an appropriate threshold is met. Extensive experiments confirm that ShotPruner significantly outperforms state-of-the-re methods across various configurations and benchmark datasets.

This work examines ADS and U(1) non-invertible symmetries within d-dimensional free fermion theories, alongside a fully coupled (1+1)-dimensional UV model that exhibits the Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly. We characterize the corresponding symmetry condensate theory by utilizing the duality between the fermionic theory and the worldsheet theory of free Dirac material strings. Furthermore, the analysis reveals the role of the 3-cohomology group U(1) within the 2-group structure of the ADS symmetry.

We present TaueganBayes (TaueganBayesB), a tool for classifying variable time-variant astronomical events based on time-variant color-color state diagrams, utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Testing on real data confirmed that TaueganBayesB matches the accuracy of existing filters while providing per-event uncertainty metrics to aid future candidate refinement.

Predicting churn within the online gambling sector is a critical area of research with direct economic consequences. This study addresses the challenge of identifying customers who will abandon the platform using neural networks. The proposed method begins by extracting transaction-derived features and employing them to train various deep learning models to forecast customer churn. We assess these networks based on classification accuracy and efficiency, focusing on accuracy metrics such as precision, recall, the F1-score, and the Area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve. Our results indicate that a residual multilayer perceptron network outperforms other architectures in classifying the targets, while simultaneously delivering the rapid inference speeds necessary for real-time applications.

This work investigates the Ising Field Theory (IFT) using non-rational Conformal Field Theory (CFT) methods. We demonstrate that the dominant singular behavior close to the Yang-Lee edge singularity in theories containing unitary CFT is governed by a fixed point described by an $sl(2,\mathbb{C})$ current algebra at a specific central charge, denoted as $c$. We propose that IFT can be formulated through non-rational CFT on a specific character lattice, yielding an automorphic representation of $sl(2,\mathbb{C})$. Furthermore, the model incorporates two distinct conformal families, each characterized by primary weights of $(\pm\frac{1}{2}, \pm\frac{1}{2})$ that generate two isotropic spin fields. Consequently, the corresponding field representations are $\mathbb{C}^2$. The action of the lattice automorphism group, $av(\mathbb{Z}_{\mathbb{Z}})$, upon the conformal families is linked to the $\mathbb{Z}_{\mathbb{Z}}$-symmetry of the spin fields. Consequently, the associated field representations are $\mathbb{Z}_{\mathbb{Z}}$. Finally, the one-loop renormalization group flow leads directly to the Gaussian model.

We establish that gluon TMDPDFs are essential for the analysis of gluons through their role in transverse-polarization distributions, highlighting their significance in both experimental applications and theoretical frameworks involving spin physics. Furthermore, the study presents the theoretical structure of these functions, the evolution equations for gluon TMDs, the resulting predictions for specific observables involving gluons, and the relevant parton-to-gluon matching conditions required for accurate data interpretation within the framework of quantum chromodynamics and lattice gauge theory.

Photon-photon interactions in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions (URHICs) can generate electron-positron pairs, which subsequently interact with the medium to produce real quasi-free photons. This study examines ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions in a quark-gluon plasma environment using a three-component kinetic approach that accounts for the ultra-relativistic contributions of these thermal photons. We derive an analytical formula for the frequency-dependent spectral function of thermal photons and calculate their contribution to the average yield. Additionally, results are presented regarding the influence of plasma electrons and positrons on this thermal photon spectrum. Our findings indicate that this photon component represents a minor contribution to the total yield of thermal photons observed in URHICs.

Developing cycling route-assistance tools depends on accurately evaluating risks associated with different segments. Traditional models often estimate these risks by aggregating historical accident data with contextual elements like road geometry and traffic volume. In this paper, we introduce an image-based methodology that classifies route segments using data from a single sensor source: cameras. Leveraging the widespread nature of cycling GPS trackers, rich visual data collection is common, yet image data is typically underutilized in risk modeling. Our findings indicate that using deep neural networks to process route image segments yields performance comparable to conventional methods. However, adopting our framework offers superior scalability and adaptability. Unlike methods constrained by the need for accident histories, this approach can differentiate between accident types and generalize to new regions without retraining on local accident records.

Control Barrier Functions (CBF) offer a viable approach to planning robot movements that keep specific safe states accessible. However, when obstacles shift over time, ensuring a robust CBF becomes computationally difficult because the required non-quadratic constraints hinder pathfinding. To address this, we present a new adaptive technique to convert time-variant quadratic constraints into static equivalents without sacrificing accuracy, utilizing these functions to guarantee access to all targets within defined safety zones. By combining adaptive adjustments with probabilistic methods, we prove that the resulting closed-loop system maintains stochastic stability. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method's performance is superior compared to previously proposed techniques through both simulations and real-world experiments.

Dilation surfaces serve as a natural extension of translation surfaces, where flat square tori are arranged in a polygon with identifications via vector translations, replaced here by linear dilations. The resulting directional dynamics on these surfaces yield orbit-trace pairs forming a countable collection of Borel measure sets; however, unlike translation scenarios, these dilation flow traces lack countable invariance under dilation. The present analysis addresses fundamental questions regarding the absolute continuity and singular nature of this measure, as well as the uniform distribution of orbits. Dilation surfaces emerge from the study of printed circuit boards under electromagnetic influence; they also encompass flat, infinite, topologically Euclidean graphs known as leptotich surfaces.

Recent research has suggested using Total Correlation (TC) as a more effective metric than standard functional connectivity measures to capture the multidimensional nature of brain activity. This approach allows for reasonable, nonparametric estimation of TC even in scenarios with a large number of variables relative to sample size, provided the variables are multivariate Gaussian. However, this assumption proves problematic for TC estimation in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data due to the presence of non-physiological correlations among blood flow signals in the same region. To address this, we develop a new TC estimator tailored for such correlated time series, employing a partial covariance structure to eliminate redundancies. Furthermore, we apply this method to assess TC among large-scale brain activity patterns. Additionally, we validate our findings through simulations, which demonstrate a clear distinction in TC values between healthy subjects and those with Alzheimer's disease.

While classical Segal-Bargmann theory employs irreducible unitary representations of the Heisenberg-Weyl group to link continuous-variable quantum mechanics with free stochastic calculus, our work extends this framework to specific subsets of the special linear group, denoted as $SL(n,\mathbb{R})$. These subsets correspond to trajectories within a modified phase space featuring a reduced dimension. Consequently, these representations facilitate a mapping from $n$-dimensional free stochastic calculus to the dimerized quantum mechanics of $n$-mode systems. A secondary objective involves exploring the emergence of wave-particle duality through the use of Fock space representations and Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) constructions. These approaches utilize Fock-space realizations to generate unitary groups that act as the operators necessary for formalizing wave-particle duality.

In Bayesian analyses, Gaussian process (GP) analyses are common, yet their posterior distributions over covariance functions are high-dimensional and intricate, making exact sampling impossible and rendering standard Monte Carlo methods impractical due to prohibitive computational costs. We introduce GP-SAM, a novel simulation algorithm designed to efficiently generate samples from the GP posterior distribution over covariance functions. GP-SAM achieves this by leveraging shared structural properties within this specific posterior class. The method performs a Monte Carlo simulation that depends only on the GP noise variance and maintains constant simulation duration regardless of training set size. Furthermore, the computational burden for each generated sample is minimal, requiring O(d³) operations where d represents the dimensionality of the covariance function's domain. This study presents measurements and analysis of wireless dipole antenna pattern ground patterns in outdoor settings, covering from close proximity to far-field conditions. The author found that when the ground is perfectly reflective, the resulting pattern closely matches observed data in most outdoor cases. Additionally, the paper evaluates the impact of ground surface roughness on near-field and far-field radiation patterns.

The recent observation of neutrino oscillations at the Fermilab Neutrino Discovery Experiment has opened a new frontier in understanding the mixing and flavor oscillation of neutrinos. This phenomenon is further examined through the lens of the Iron Cherenkov Telescope Array, which is designed to observe ultra-high-energy neutrinos. By utilizing iron absorbers, the array can effectively distinguish between the flavor characteristics of neutrinos and neutrinos, allowing their mixing to be studied in a regime where the energy scale of the ultra-High-Energy neutrinos provides a distinct advantage. This region of the neutrino spectrum is particularly significant because it may reveal new physics beyond the Standard Model, thereby extending the research initiated by the low-energy observations of oscillations to the most extreme energies possible.

Top quarks are crucial for exploring physics beyond the standard model. This paper provides a framework for detecting standard model violations using the associated production of top quarks and bottom quarks, analyzed through the lens of the effective field theory. We establish that the most effective way to constrain new physics in the top-bottom system is to enforce unitarity on anomalous top quark decays. Our methodology, based on LHC Run 2 datasets, includes a comprehensive, systematic comparison between limiting results expressed in Lattice Wilson coefficients and constraints derived from the effective field theory approach.

In the context of reinforcement learning, classical experience replay functions as an off-policy technique that facilitates training by aggregating past transitions and treating random data access as the most suitable strategy. While this approach is suboptimal, as replaying earlier data from the same state distribution hinders learning efficiency, recent findings suggest that prioritizing samples based on absolute frequency can overcome these limitations. This paper introduces Prioritized Retrievable Experience (PRE), a novel prioritized experience replay method designed for both model-based and model-free settings. Rather than relying on static pre-trained distributions, PRE dynamically identifies high-priority samples within a moving state distribution derived from ongoing policy updates, effectively utilizing a dynamic counter for sample importance. We evaluate PRE across three standard benchmarks for both model-free and model-based algorithms, demonstrating that it consistently surpasses existing prioritized methods in terms of effectiveness and achieving state-of-the-art performance in many scenarios.

Spatiotemporal predictive learning (ST-PL) aims to anticipate future frames based on prior ones, a capability widely used in vision systems for enhancing the frame rates of commercial cameras. A key challenge remains that achieving high prediction accuracy typically demands extensive computational resources, rendering these systems unsuitable for deployment on devices with limited processing power. To address this, we introduce a novel local ST-PL approach designed to minimize prediction errors while significantly cutting down on computations. The strategy involves three main components: utilizing frame patches for localized computations, developing a novel loss function to guide the learning process, and implementing a self-adaptive mechanism that optimizes the predictions of future outputs. Experiments conducted on the public SpaceNet dataset confirm that this low-compute method not outperforms existing models in accuracy but also substantially reduces the computational workload.

This study investigates the feasibility of implementing demand-driven memory allocation in functional programming. Traditionally, functional languages utilize continuous-memory schemes that postpone garbage collection. In contrast, continuous schemes struggle with parallel environments where multiple collectors compete; splitting memory significantly reduces collector efficiency, whereas localized continuous collectors fail to collect widely dispersed continuous memory segments. Consequently, this research examines whether physical memory can be managed via discrete intervals—specifically frames—under a demand-driven framework. The proposed approach acquires data only upon immediate need and pre-allocates subsequent frames ahead of time. The findings indicate that utilizing pre-allocated frames can enhance garbage collection performance in parallel contexts.

This study presents a first-principles thermodynamic analysis designed to assess the fracture toughness of crystalline materials. We established the fundamental equations linking fracture toughness with critical thermodynamic variables, such as crack extension force and critical crack extension work. Furthermore, our work derived the theoretical relationship between fracture toughness and dislocation density; this relationship indicates that as material strength increases, the influence of dislocation density becomes less significant. Within this same equation lies the crucial "dislocation diffusion distance," a parameter that quantifies the extent over which fracture processes remain influenced by dislocation density. The proposed models serve as an excellent foundation for formulating new empirical formulas for measuring fracture toughness.

Building upon the demonstration in [arXiv:2006.02727] that the Gaussian free field (GFF) can be viewed as a "polarization" of any stochastic process, I investigate the relationship between GFFs and their corresponding "depolarized" realizations. Additionally, I address the "discrete" counterpart introduced in [arXiv:1907.03122] as a continuous-time random walk with depinning dynamics. The study explores the connection between this depolarized model and the GFF, with an overarching goal of deriving universal characteristics and key results for both the Aizenman-Molchanow framework and the Gaussian model by analyzing them through the lens of depinning and stochastic field theory.

The task of efficiently verifying quantum computation is becoming increasingly critical, particularly now that large quantum processors capable of massive state outputs are emerging. While recent advancements have optimized interactive proofs for these scenarios, they still rely on basic verification methods where a classical server simply checks measurement results in the computational basis, a step currently known to incur a high information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(T \log T)$ bit transmission for running a circuit with $T$ gates. This study introduces a novel protocol for the single-server scenario that surpasses the previous state-of-the-art efficiency, requiring only $\mathcal O(T \log T \log(1/\delta))$ classical bits to achieve a soundness error probability of $\delta$ for any polynomial $2$-qubit gate circuit. Notably, the protocol's underlying security relies on planting quantum keys within two-key trapped states, validated via single-photon measurements, under assumptions that plausibly hold in standard post-quantum cryptographic settings.

Blockchain technology has emerged as a prominent solution in crypto economics, with growing interest in its application to IoT within scholarly research. However, standard blockchains face significant scalability and computational challenges that conventional protocols struggle to address effectively. Consequently, scholars have been developing specialized, tailored IoT blockchains to mitigate these limitations. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of existing IoT blockchain systems, categorizing them according to the specific IoT application domains they target.

We introduce a machine learning framework designed to learn cell shapes through the level sets of signed distance functions (SDFs). This approach surpasses voxel-based methods, which are limited by low resolution, and polygon meshes, which lack smoothness. By utilizing SDFs to capture smooth, implicit representations of complex 3D shapes, the model leverages convolutional neural networks to detect local geometric patterns. These networks process grid inputs—such as voxel fields or level set maps—to output continuous value estimates. This architecture successfully identifies irregular surface irregularities and infers topology even when input data is incomplete. Furthermore, the framework achieves state-of-the-art results in predicting cell volume and total surface area from 2D cross-sections. This capability enables the three-dimensional reconstruction of cells from sparse 2D slices, demonstrating the system's utility in handling partially obscured and fragmented data scenarios.

Printed materials often present obstacles to the development of print-dependent literacy among the visually impaired. To address this, we introduce an end-to-end architecture that detects and tracks the lines within a multi-line document featuring a curved baseline, processing the output frame-by-frame in real time. Our system utilizes an end-to-end deep learning system comprising a convolutional neural network (CNN) for detection and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) for tracking. While such end-to-end approaches have previously been limited to single-line scenarios, this approach is distinct for handling complex curvature in time-sensitive contexts. We validate our method across various documents, including flat and curved parallel sheets as well as multi-layer curvilinear baselines. Additionally, we have established the first-ever public dataset dedicated to the tracking of curvilinear baselines.

This report introduces an improved language model, referred to as XLNet, built on the premise that pre-training should effectively capture the distributional representations of language in a language model, a goal we argue XLNet achieves. In contrast to BERT, our method applies the fully contextual encoding strategy to the original token order rather than reversing it with tokenization, a technique that enables more effective modeling of discrete language distributions. Our proposed approach employs joint learning of both token assignments and token identities, a process that can occur in an autoregressive fashion, thus utilizing all available information from the input context in XLNet. In addition, our method utilizes a new predictive approach, allowing the model to predict the missing tokens in a given sequence. In a series of experiments, we demonstrate that this new method can achieve better performance than BERT in tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, and coreference resolution. Our results show that XLNet can achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of natural language processing tasks.

In this study, we offer a detailed analysis of the interface locomotion of the millipede *L. forficatus. Although this invertebrate is known for its terrestrial running capabilities, it uniquely moves across the air-water interface by using surface tension-driven surface skimming. To understand this specific behavior, we conducted high-speed videography sessions and applied image processing to capture the animal's dynamics. Our findings indicate a strong correlation between the propulsive forces and the size of the meniscus generated by feet impacting the surface. Furthermore, we calculated swimming velocity by examining the interaction between foot-meniscus dynamics and the resulting hydrodynamic and interfacial resistances. Theoretical modeling and analysis demonstrate that the organism maintains stability and achieves propulsion by utilizing propulsion through asynchronous menisci and distributing reactive stresses. Ultimately, this research provides significant insights into the biomechanics of animal movement at both liquid-air and water interfaces.

We report the discovery of a cluster containing 11 HST-dark galaxies within the COSMOS field, utilizing the S4 survey's ultra-deep WISE W3 band data. These galaxies exhibit redshifts between 2.2 and 3.3 and reside at a mean physical projected distance of 1.1 Mpc from the nearby SMACS J0136.1−2117 cluster. For the first time, we have established the properties of this specific population, determining that they possess stellar masses between $10^{9}$ and $10^{9.5} M_{\odot}$, and span a star formation rate range of $0.1$ to $10 M_{\odot} \text{yr}^{-1}$. Their dust properties closely resemble those of the well-studied S0222 population, with a median far-infrared to ultraviolet ratio ($SFR/100~\mu m$) of $0.00001$. Additionally, their dust emission profiles mirror those of the S0222 group, characterized by strong central peaks and extended outer emission. This suggests that dust in these galaxies is likely produced by galaxy-merger events and cosmic feedback mechanisms.

We investigate seven-dimensional gravity incorporating specific topological terms defined by linear combinations of four- and six-form components, resulting in modified Einstein field equations. By solving these equations for static, spherically-symmetric black holes, we demonstrate the existence of a one-parameter family, characterized by an arbitrary mass. Introducing rotation through the Neugebauer-Chappert framework yields another one-parameter family of solutions corresponding to angular momentum. Furthermore, by linear superposition, we construct configurations of multiple spheres. The analysis extends to stationary, axially-symmetric spacetimes, where we identify a family of five-parameter solutions featuring two angular momenta and two independent phases.

This study investigates the characteristics of disks constrained within narrow pathways using discrete event simulations. Our primary focus lies in contrastingly examining two distinct dimensions of "jamming": the macro level, governed by initial configurations and disk sequencing, and the fine detail, determined by micro-scale disk rearrangements. Consequently, our research demonstrates that both aspects are crucial; specific sequences of entries and subtle positional shifts both significantly influence final jammed states. Furthermore, by enumerating all unique disk permutations for systems involving just 6 disks, our work reveals how entrance order and alignment orientation dictate the resulting macro-scale geometry in the jammed configuration.

The historical record indicates two distinct types of El Niño: one characterized by warming in the eastern Pacific and another by central Pacific warming. While previous research has highlighted their divergent global impacts, this study specifically examines their contrasting effects on global seasonal rainfall. Utilizing a 50-year dataset of observed seasonal precipitation combined with reanalysis El Niño indices, the analysis reveals that the traditional East Pacific type strongly suppresses precipitation across the northwestern Pacific and Southwestern Indian oceans, simultaneously triggering droughts in the subtropics of southern Africa and southern South America and fueling increased rainfall in the northeastern Pacific. Conversely, the Central Pacific type dampens moisture levels in the subtropical regions of northern and southern South America, southern Africa, and northeastern Russia, while boosting rainfall in the northeastern Southwestern Indian oceans and the northeastern Southwestern South America. A defining difference lies in the East Pacific type's ability to enhance rainfall in the northeastern northwestern Pacific sector, a response absent in the Central Pacific variant. These findings underscore significant regional disparities in how these El Niño modes alter extratropical precipitation patterns.

Although taxonomies are highly useful for representing product information and facilitating recommendation systems, accurately modeling their hierarchical nature in Euclidean space remains challenging. To address this, we introduce TaxoHub, a novel unsupervised method for embedding taxonomy into hyperbolic space. This approach successfully captures hyperbolic clustering and preserves Euclidean proximity. The system also handles the dynamic addition of new nodes without retraining, making it well-su to evolving taxonomies. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation on numerous real-world datasets demonstrates that TaxoHub produces embeddings which outperform both standard and previous methods in both global accuracy and the fidelity of the hierarchical structure.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution has intensified global competition, compelling companies to optimize their decision-making processes. However, delays and inaccurate budgeting often stem from the complexity and unpredictability of making choices under uncertainty in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, this research proposes a meta-heuristic algorithm that integrates both probabilistic and imprecise data to support Company A, a logistics firm, in optimizing a replenishment problem. The objective is to select the optimal number of suppliers, their purchasing quantities, and delivery timing. While several mathematical approaches exist for this replenishment problem, they frequently rely on restrictive or unrealistic assumptions. Consequently, we have introduced a multi-criteria fuzzy bi-heuristic algorithm, which is the first of its kind to address such a scenario. By utilizing fuzzy logic and DNA computing, the system can manage fuzzy numbers and assess risk profiles, resulting in the generation of diverse non-dominated solutions. The effectiveness of this model was validated through a case study using non-existent data, with outcomes visualized to demonstrate that the proposed strategy is both viable and effective.

Resiliency is increasingly recognized as a vital attribute for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), enabling them to function effectively despite unannounced attacks. While the field has advanced significantly in recent years, the development of a rigorous mathematical framework for resiliency remains an open challenge. This study introduces a model-based approach designed to quantify resiliency, applicable to diverse systems within the CPS domain. A novel framework, grounded in control theory and embedded systems, is established to model disruptive events and subsequent recovery efforts. Utilizing this framework to analyze a specific metric for a given system, we derive both lower and upper bounds for its resilience. Furthermore, we apply an optimal control framework to maximize resiliency by determining the ideal disruption and recovery strategies. To ensure practical application, a non-linear, bi-level optimization problem formulated for this purpose exhibits tractable characteristics. As demonstration, a case study involving an autonomous vehicle is presented, utilizing the framework to both quantify a specific resiliency profile and identify the most resilient scenarios.

Dark matter remains a major unsolved problem in physics, with leading hypotheses identifying it as either axions or WIMPs. We have recently created a new approach to locate dark matter self-axions through their possible interaction with photons, specifically in a "laboratory" environment rather than an astrophysical setting. This method, known as SHiPPIR, operates without the restrictive constraints typically applied to similar searches. The distinctive advantage of this work is that the energy levels of "lab" dark matter can be precisely controlled and measured, allowing for a significantly broader mass range to be investigated. We aim to provide an overview of this unique concept and its associated experimental design.

This article presents a unified framework encompassing various stochastic process (SP) optimal control problems (OCPs). In this setting, Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), which include numerous well-known systems such as time series analysis, are mathematically described as sequences $X^n = (X_t)_{t \in \{0,\dots,n\}}$ governed by a probability measure $\mathbb{P}^*$ on a measurable space $(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{B})$. These models are utilized to characterize the characteristics $Z_t \,(\equiv Z(Z,\mathcal{B}))$ observed as measurements. Based on these observations, one must solve an HMM-based OCP to select an action $a_t$ that minimizes the expected cumulative cost over a horizon $n$. This paper derives the dynamic programming equations for such an OCPs, demonstrating their equivalence to solving the minimization problem directly under an appropriate cost structure and establishing conditions under which the value function converges as $n \to \infty$. Furthermore, the analysis investigates the asymptotic behavior of the value function and links these results to minimization problems in information theory and statistical estimation.

This work analyzes a class of advection dynamics driven by a basis function truncated within an infinite-dimensional, colored, stationary Gaussian field. The corresponding flow map and associated characteristics are demonstrated to possess a frame-theoretical representation. Consequently, the resulting frame transforms are utilized alongside theoretical analysis to reveal the fractal nature inherent to the turbulence model described.

We introduce a technique to fit nuclear elastic scattering data that avoids reliance on an a priori folding model. Instead of specifying a model, an effective potential is derived by freely adjusting a polynomial with real coefficients, ensuring positivity, differentiability, and symmetry. This generated potential is subsequently used for calculating orbital angular momentum ($l$)-dependent optical potentials via an energy-based expansion. We demonstrate that accuracy in predicting the calculated polynomial at unseen energies and configurations is markedly enhanced through the simultaneous fitting across various energies and to differential cross-section data. We further show that the resulting optimal $l$-dependent optical potentials yield significantly improved predictions of scattering differential cross-sections spanning a broad energy range, when compared to earlier models. These findings confirm that models selected by the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC) provide a robust framework valid across extensive conditions for predicting scattering differential cross-sections.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of electromagnetic radiation confined within a one-dimensional vacuum cavity (thin slab). Utilizing both quantum and fully classical frameworks, we calculate radiation energy levels and derive expressions for energy, entropy, and pressure. Our results reveal a distinct temperature-dependent transition: at low temperatures, the system mimics an ultracold gas of massive particles, whereas at high temperatures, it behaves as standard classical blackbody radiation.

Offering meaningful location privacy for LBS users becomes significantly more complex when many positions are exposed within brief intervals, a scenario typical for mobile devices. Existing research primarily employs adaptive privacy techniques that analyze user trajectories across successive locations to construct personal models. Based on these models, the system can then apply granular, location-specific privacy policies. This process hinges on the accuracy of the generated models, as their reliability directly impacts the strength of the assigned privacy protections. This study investigates the precision limitations inherent in such personal models. Our analysis demonstrates that even with access to extensive location data, the accuracy of models built using conventional methods—standard in the field today—remains surprisingly low. This finding suggests that current approaches may inadvertently grant excessive privacy access to users, highlighting a critical need for improved modeling techniques.

Autonomous driving heavily relies on 3D point cloud-based place recognition, a capability essential for tasks like loop-closure detection in GPS-denied settings. However, the presence of drivable areas introduces significant challenges due to large intra-class variations and small inter-class differences within input point clouds. To address this, we introduce a new method that integrates geometric and semantic features for robust place recognition through deep learning. Specifically, we utilize a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract semantic features from point cloud data, paired with a dedicated network to learn an effective feature descriptor from these semantic outputs. Crucially, this learned descriptor incorporates geometric information implicitly, thereby enhancing recognition accuracy even when GPS signals are unavailable. Extensive experiments conducted on the TU Munich 6D dataset confirm that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving strong performance through this efficient strategy.

Multisite investigations are increasingly vital for investigating resting-state functional connectivity; however, distinct sites often exhibit varying functional profiles, introducing noise that threatens statistical power. This study evaluates the efficacy of multisite designs over single-site setups regarding group effect detection in such data. Using data from the 1000 Functional Connections Project (a combined sample of 1,188 participants across four centers), the authors conducted single-sample t-tests across 160 conditions (comparing age versus gender at each site versus the pooled dataset) to assess relative power. Results indicated that multisite testing yielded lower power for these specific conditions compared to single-site testing. Despite this trend, the observed power differences were statistically insignificant, indicating similar power levels regardless of the testing scope. The authors attribute the lack of significant difference between multisite and single-site power to the fact that remaining between-site variance was comparable to within-subject variance. Consequently, the study concludes that resting-fMRI research can achieve equivalent results in both single-site and multisite frameworks, provided data aggregation strategies are managed appropriately.

Density functional calculations combined with the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg formalism were employed to examine the relationship between pressure and critical temperature ($T_c$) for H$_{3}$S. Unlike earlier studies suggesting $T_c$ is independent of pressure, our results indicate an initially linear increase in $T_c$ with pressure up to approximately 200 GPa, followed by saturation, a trend consistent with recent experimental data for pressures reaching 260 GPa. This behavior is explained by a strong dependence of the density of states at the Fermi level on energy. This paper introduces a new motion planning framework designed for dynamic environments that rely solely on local sensors. Its primary advantage is real-time performance, circumventing the need for environment-wide mapping required by map-dependent global planners. The approach utilizes a probabilistic method tailored for environments with unknown geometry, projecting potential paths from the robot's current location based on immediate local data. Path selection is governed by a probability distribution derived from a physics-informed machine learning model that forecasts the trajectories of dynamic objects. This specific model is trained on 2D camera data captured in real dynamic settings, offering fast, accurate predictions of both geometry and physics, including the prediction of free space and object motion patterns. Furthermore, the probabilistic generator is enhanced with a learned reward function that prioritizes paths with superior physical realism. Empirical results from actual environments demonstrate that the robot successfully avoids known and unknown dynamic obstacles, achieving successful navigation tasks in 90% of scenarios, while maintaining the flexibility to operate in areas where a prior map does not exist.

This paper addresses the challenge of visual relocalization within general settings. We propose a novel approach utilizing compact 3D surfel maps and a specialized rendering method to create an adaptable database suitable for relocalization. To query this database, we present a new patch matching algorithm that leverages keypoint and line descriptors alongside surfel geometric data. These geometric constraints enhance the robustness of the system against challenges such as field-of-view limitations and specular reflections by using surfels to match corresponding planes. Furthermore, various optimization techniques based on surfel geometry are employed to extract robust features and refine these features further. Our evaluation on the NYU v2 dataset for 3D surfel mapping, as well as the Visual Localization 1-D and 2-D Datasets for relocalization, emulates realistic camera fields using a driver from an actual vehicle. Results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the 3D surfel and localization benchmarks.

Federated learning (FL) represents a vital framework for training machine learning models across distributed data while ensuring data privacy. Flatttened FL involves aggregating data from entities with identical records horizontally, whereas vertical FL complements this by involving entities with identical columns locally. Existing research has primarily focused on optimizing FL efficiency specifically within one paradigm. This paper introduces Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Data (LHV), a novel setting that integrates varying data characteristics into classical FL configurations. In LHV, multiple federated participants possess datasets that do not strictly align horizontally or vertically; instead, each participant holds a unique combination of both rows and columns relative to the others. Each participant trains a local model on their specific subset of rows and columns before sending only the global updates to a central aggregator, which merges these into a unified model for all data. To our knowledge, this is the first approach to address FL in this distinctive heterogeneous landscape. We will explore potential scenarios for LHV and outline a framework along with a comparative analysis contrasting it with existing FL approaches. Furthermore, we will evaluate the performance of LHV against traditional FL settings.

This study introduces a distance-based control (DBC) framework for platoon management in a connected and automated vehicle (CAV) environment, utilizing two distinct information structures: constant spacing based on relative distance and constant time-based distance. The objective is to eliminate oscillations caused by "ghost effects"—driving errors introduced by human operators through the vehicle line—even under delayed and noisy sensor data conditions. To achieve this, we employ a Lyapunov-Krasovskii approach within the linear time-invariant framework combined with state-dependent delay techniques, ensuring stability conditions are satisfied. Subsequently, a precise state-dependent delay model is formulated based on human driver behavior, allowing for the formal verification that this specific delay ensures system stability. Finally, numerical simulations confirm the proposed state-dependent delay model and validate the efficacy of the overall DBC scheme.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) remains the primary workhorse for training machine models, though its standard implementation necessitates a communication-intensive loop between data processing and weight updates. This paper introduces a novel technique, Communication-Avoiding Stochastic Gradient Descent (CA-SGD), which retains the local parallelization and scalability of traditional SGD while eliminating the redundant communications inherent in that framework. CA-SGD was initially validated within multi-class linear classification but can readily be extended to highly parallelized non-linear models such as deep neural networks. Theoretically, we prove that CA-SGD maintains convergence to a $\epsilon$-accurate solution with the same iteration complexity as standard SGD. Empirically, simulations across 2,048 and 8 processors demonstrate a speedup of up to 3.3x and 2.4x respectively for CA-SGD when compared to traditional SGD.

The rapid advancement of computer science has facilitated an unprecedented increase in computer-generated content, notably through automated headline generation by algorithms. This innovation has, unfortunately, enabled the widespread dissemination of false news, creating challenges for individuals in distinguishing real information from computer-fabricated headlines. This paper introduces the sentiment analysis of computer-generated false news, specifically examining its association with tone through our proposed Sentiment Headline Fake News (SHFN) framework. Our approach leverages data from the Google Custom Search API alongside ground-trusted information from reputable publications. Additionally, we evaluate several pre-trained BERT models within our framework to assess their effectiveness in analyzing the sentiment and direction of false news.

Radio interferometers generate a vast quantity of data, necessitating specialized hardware to reduce the computational load of calculating correlations from antenna pairs. While an FFT-based architecture can perform these operations in $O(N \log N)$ time—compared to $O(N^2)$ for conventional correlators—this approach requires a duration of $T \log T$ seconds to complete $N$ FFTs over a total time $T$. Furthermore, such systems demand that the observation duration be broken into discrete segments of equal length. This work introduces a new method utilizing a single window function to continuously model correlations in real-time as they occur, eliminating the need for segmented observations. The method was validated using data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) with VIPSERV software, producing results that match standard FFT-corr results to within 0.001%.

Although the original C Markov Chain Monte Carlo (C MCMC) algorithm has been widely used in financial time series modeling, this study introduces a novel integration of Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGANs) to replace C MCMC as an effective generative model. The objective is to generate time series data that accurately reproduces the statistical properties of the S&P 500 index. To evaluate this approach, we propose a comprehensive methodology designed to rigorously compare model performance. The research demonstrates that this new evaluation framework is superior to conventional testing procedures for assessing generative models, specifically regarding financial time series. Furthermore, this methodology enables a more robust analysis of model reliability by effectively eliminating any bias stemming from historical data. Finally, this investigation establishes that C MCMC algorithms can be enhanced by substituting the traditional rejection sampling technique with CGAN-generated samples. Consequently, this research suggests that CGANs serve as a superior alternative to C MCMC for improving generative models in financial time series applications.

The calculation for $A_{\mathcal{O}}^{(3)}$ represents a significant theoretical advancement in understanding the behavior of polarized quarks in the context of high-energy scattering processes.

This study utilizes machine learning techniques to classify newly identified Fermi-LAT blazar candidates. The classification distinguishes between BL Lacertae-type and other types of active galactic nuclei based on multi-wavelength data, leveraging both non-imaging and imaging instruments surrounding the source. The developed classifier was evaluated using various testing strategies, achieving a 90% accuracy rate. The analysis also examined how including different data features influences classification reliability and assessed how well the model could anticipate the source fluxes in specific wavelength bands.

Mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) analysis is commonly employed in clinical trials to evaluate continuous outcomes. In practical application, time is frequently modeled as a categorical variable representing specific study visits. However, this approach can introduce bias or loss of statistical power if patients have not yet reached certain scheduled visits due to discontinuation, leaving missing data points at those later time points. To mitigate the impact of such incomplete observations, the MMRM model must utilize a sufficient amount of pre-climb information regarding the missing mechanisms. While MMRM with categorical time offers robust, valid inferences under a missing at random (MAR) assumption, this assumption often proves unrealistic for many clinical trials. A more flexible alternative allows time to be modeled as a continuous variable using actual follow-up dates instead of discrete categorical levels. This strategy generally enhances power and, when combined with appropriate analysis covariates, offers greater flexibility in addressing missing data patterns. This paper compares the statistical properties and performance of MMRM under both assumptions through a comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation.

Designed for the identification of reaction pathways, the LSM action represents an extension of Freidlin-Wentzell theory to discrete systems. It quantifies the likelihood of transition trajectories during a small noise-driven perturbation, provided certain discrete system constraints are met. However, applying this to active matter presents challenges due to the presence of a preferred direction in velocity space, the discrete nature of time, and an inherent time-scale separation. This study addresses these complexities by deriving an active matter-specific form of the LSM action, first for general speed biasing and then for systems maintaining mechanical balance under external driving forces.

We present novel insights into the theoretical limits of input-output polymathtomatic regular functions. First, the polyregular functions are defined as the closure under composition for polynomial mappings derived from polynomial-sized finite automata. Second, the exact computational complexity of these polyregular functions is precisely determined. Third, the existence of a finitary grammar system for polyregular functions is proven, with applications to the description complexity of languages. Fourth, the description complexity of these functions is shown to be exponentially bounded in terms of the size of the input alphabet. Finally, the description complexity of polyregular functions is tightly bounded, with upper and lower limits differing only logarithmically. The results presented here have significant applications to the description complexity of languages.

This paper answers whether a topological space's primativity—defined here as a certain global constraint ensuring all normal subgroups are prime given that the local stabilizers are connected—necessarily implies connectedness. Furthermore, the authors provide a characterization of when such a topological group is locally lacunital under the assumption of primativity.

This study introduces a fine-tuning approach for cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing that targets domain name and table column identification. The proposed method employs two auxiliary loss functions to independently refine these components, thereby circumventing the need for large-scale supervised datasets. By leveraging few-shot settings, our approach exploits the potential in data efficiency within such settings. Extensive experiments on two databases from the SQLBenchmark dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in isolated columns and tables, especially within cross-domain scenarios.

Ensuring safe navigation remains a critical aspect of collaborative robot systems. This paper presents a safety-aware navigation framework designed for groups of robots, leveraging a constrained Markov decision process (MDP) model where the transition dynamics and cost functions are subject to uncertainty. To address these uncertainties, the authors utilize conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), a robust risk metric, to construct a constrained Markov decision process that guarantees safe operation. Under specific assumptions regarding probability distributions, distributionally robust CVaR can be recast as a Markov decision process with linear constraints; consequently, the original problem reduces to solving this specific MDP variant. An efficient solution is obtained using a policy iteration framework with value function representations based on piecewise-linear convex functions, alongside a dedicated update rule for valuing terminal states. Furthermore, the approach facilitates the generation of a terminal state valuation capable of approximating the optimal objective function for the problem. Numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the method's efficacy in achieving safety-valued navigation within mixed human-robot environments.

Grant-free communication (GF) offers a promising solution for massive machine-type communications (mMTC) by eliminating the need for individual device authorization. Within this framework, sparse and low-rate data transmitted by numerous devices must be recovered despite challenges such as severe user activity detection issues and inter-user interference. This study investigates the performance limits of GF systems by analyzing transmission rates and the number of simultaneously active devices. Specifically, we examine two scenarios: one assuming perfect channel state information at the receiver and another accounting for an imperfect channel estimate receiver, alongside the receiver's uncertainty regarding total device counts. By applying information-theoretic tools, we derive an upper bound on the number of active devices for a given error probability and determine the maximum achievable data rate per device. These theoretical derivations are validated through simulations.

The paper presents a new Lagrangian model specifically developed to describe the thermodynamics of moist air. Unlike many existing approaches, this model rigorously applies the conservation of the thermodynamic potential using the total differential without relying on the Gibbs-Dalton law, which many other models require. This formulation ensures the compatibility of the model's equations with the classical first and second laws of thermodynamics. It explicitly accounts for the irreversible mixing of dry air and water vapor through a specific partial differential equation governing potential temperature evolution. Furthermore, the advancement includes applying a backward finite difference scheme to a numerical simulation, resulting in an algorithm designed to trace the saturation cycle. This saturation cycle involves saturation condensation followed by evaporations from the supersaturated state back to saturation.

By utilizing both CN intermediate metrics and CN-based features, this research demonstrates improved results in both simulated and actual scenarios. Specifically, using simulated turn-level intent classification, CN-derived features were shown to enhance classification accuracy. Finally, this work proposes real-time ASR and intent classification systems, showing that this approach leads to more accurate responses and a better user experience.

Constructing supermoduli spaces and defining integration measures for both objects forms the basis of our construction. We establish enumerative formulas for the first category using local extensions of the gluing technique, noting that this methodology aligns with existing results regarding moduli spaces of stable curves. Furthermore, state sums over a supermoduli space representing the general case (covering edge sheaves arbitrarily) yields enumerative space integrals compatible with topological vertex principles. Consequently, we derive multiple space integrals that evaluate the topological vertex for configurations of coherent sheaves on projective curves over specific configurations.

This study establishes exact and optimal measures for the entanglement of two-qubit states using intensity correlation measurements performed on pairs of non-maximally entangled photons. As a specific instance, it identifies an optimal protocol for precisely quantifying the entanglement of polarization-based quantum two-particle systems. Additionally, it constructs a practical method to detect entanglement within arbitrary two-qubit systems by employing fermionic projection operators as filtering masks in combination with single-photon detectors.

The dynamics of the parallel component of electric current within plasma exhibit both macroscopic and localized effects. On a large scale, current transport occurs across flux surfaces through these localized structures, specifically manifesting in electron current channels (ECCs), which consist of channels of enhanced electron temperature and reduced density. These ECCs are characterized by anomalous parallel currents, anomalous heat flux, and localized radial flows. The paper investigates the physical mechanisms driving these ECCs, encompassing both their generation and evolution. The primary focus is on analyzing the formation of these ECCs in the nonlinear regime of parallel electron drift instability. The study outlines the mechanisms responsible for this instability and reveals that these ECCs are intrinsic to the turbulent dynamics within plasma. The proposed model is validated against recent data from the JET tokamak, obtained during discharges characterized by Edge Localized Modes (ELMs).

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in image classification, yet it remains difficult to adapt existing models to new classes without compromising accuracy due to catastrophic forgetting. While prior studies primarily focus on maintaining model architecture and specific parameter updates, this research investigates a more efficient approach by freezing a pre-trained model's backbone. Leveraging a novel technique that applies noise-based filtering to class-specific features, the method simultaneously mitigates forgetting and eliminates the need for a support set. Extensive testing across three public datasets confirms that these results are comparable to existing methods, with one specific case showing a 0.5% improvement in accuracy when training ResNets on the Caltech101 dataset.

Growing social media influences have intensified concerns over hate speech, which poses serious threats to hatred and violence. Addressing this requires effective tools to identify hate speech coupled with a comprehensive understanding of its contextualvocabulary. Although previous research has extracted contextual linguistic features from parallel data to build monolingual corpora paired with hate speech annotations, such efforts have not yet created a resource covering the Spanish online hate speech landscape. To fill this gap, this paper introduces an Italian语 hateg speech contextual word dictionary. First, we present an Italian polyglot hate speech parallel dataset collected from major social platforms. Second, we describe a technique for automatically generating anti-hate speech samples in English using our European Union-licensed parallel corpus resource collection techniques. Finally, we demonstrate how to automatically generate monolingual corpora of non-hate speech samples in English using a newly proposed corpus of social media hate speech parallel datasets. The results show that our proposed corpus of Spanish social media hate speech samples is more effective in identifying hateg speech in Spanish than other models.

This study examines large-scale, heterogeneous, and small-world network models of spiking neurons. We derive a mean-field equation that governs the spiking activity at the network's boundaries and analyze the conditions required for oscillatory behavior within this framework. By varying three key parameters—the degree distribution, the coupling strength, and the degree of long-range connectivity—we explore how oscillations emerge. Specifically, we observe that increasing the width of the in-degree distribution suppresses oscillations, particularly in inhibitory-only configurations. Notably, this dependency is unique to local networks lacking extensive distant connections. In the context of small-world systems, we demonstrate that dynamic small-world architectures can both initiate and terminate neural oscillations. These findings offer valuable insights for neural systems science, emphasizing the critical roles of both average connection degrees and individual microstructural variations in determining network dynamics.

This work introduces a new technique for repairing programs using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The approach treats code correction as a synthetic challenge where a generator is trained via adversarial learning to automatically propose fixes for broken code. Our core innovation, CodeGAN, stands as a specialized framework designed to train these generators directly on raw character sequences of code. Experimental results indicate that our method successfully produces viable repairs in 20% of cases and delivers improvements of 30% to 50% in repair success rates when assisting state-of-the-art generators reliant on existing repair databases.

This study introduces a universal formula for determining the capacity region of a two-way interference channel, which involves the spectral inf-mutual information rates of mutual information gaps between linear subspaces. We demonstrate that the region's boundary is defined by a maximization of a linear combination of these mutual information gaps. The maximum achievable sum rate is determined solely by the total common and complementary common-to-private spectral entropy. We also provide an alternative formulation using the spectral modulus and mutual entropy of the difference to describe the region. We prove that this mutual entropy is non-negative, with a zero value indicating an empty capacity region, thereby providing an alternative method to verify the existence of a non-zero capacity. We also provide a method to generate a achievable rate that is within a known finite and bounded rate from the sum capacity.

This study focuses on analyzing the convergence behavior of stochastic gradient descent employing exponentially decreasing step-sizes across the entire optimization landscape. Established results confirm that when minimizing a smooth, strongly-convex function, optimizing over non-convex or non-smooth functions, or handling non-smooth, non-convex functions yields full linear convergence rates under specific conditions. Our research extends this domain by investigating stochastic gradient descent with step-sizes that decay exponentially for smooth, differentiable, and strictly concave functions. We demonstrate that this approach achieves fast convergence—a rate that surpasses both that of standard stochastic gradient descent and the deterministic case. Additionally, our numerical simulations substantiate these findings and illustrate the benefits of adaptively tuning step-sizes.

Furthermore, we show that when stored references are averaged, the resulting one-point correlation functions of magnetization satisfy a specific convolution equation. The kernel of this equation comprises a long-term average of control interactions, effectively blending the influence of both reference and control components. To mitigate respiratory motion artifacts during standard MRI scans, a dedicated free-breathing four-dimensional dual-echo sequence named DUAL was developed under the guidance of real-time respiratory signals. This approach simultaneously acquires both T1- and T2-weighted images across the entire volume. The technique incorporates dynamic slice reordering driven by respiratory input and includes automated logic to halt data collection during exhalation phases, thereby accelerating the 3D whole-lung scan. The system's image acquisition synchronization with breathing patterns was validated using synchronized retraction and expansion phantoms. A study involving 20 participants demonstrated that DUAL successfully captures a full lung scan while free-breathing over a 10-minute period, with image quality comparable to scans performed with complete hold-breath instructions. A visual review by three radiologists confirmed no significant degradation in image quality and no increase in artifacts relative to reference images. The proposed DUAL sequence is now clinically available at the Paris-Saclay Center for Imaging Research.

A primary method for compressing models involves knowledge distillation, where a trained "teacher" network trains a smaller "student" network. This process typically yields improved training accuracy for the student alongside the teacher's performance. However, a common challenge is that a student's output distributions often fail to accurately reflect those of the teacher, potentially causing misalignment. To address this, we propose an approach that optimizes the alignment between teacher and student distributions. Specifically, we introduce a regularization term into the loss function that constrains the teacher's and student's distributions to lie close to one another during training. We evaluate this distributional alignment strategy against various models and loss functions, finding that it consistently enhances the accuracy of the distilled models. Furthermore, our experiments suggest that combining our proposed alignment technique with other methods can lead to even greater improvements in overall performance.
