This study introduces a new recurrent neural architecture, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), which draws inspiration from the orthogonal polynomials utilized in control theory. By mapping recent word sequences to points on the Legendre multi-dimensional hypersphere and leveraging its associated polynomial recursion, the LMU constructs a theoretical memory space. This approach enables the neural unit to infer sequence continuations by predicting future states based on its current memory representation. We evaluated LMU against existing models, including BERT, transformer, and LSTM, across three tasks: time series forecasting, character-level synthesis for Shakespeare, and next-word prediction in the COCONLi benchmark. Results demonstrate that LMU surpasses an LSTM baseline and performs comparably to BERT and transformer models in these evaluations. Additionally, experiments reveal that LMU benefits from parallelization and exhibits robust learning behavior when the training dataset is scaled up.

The LHC's high-luminosity phase stands as the most significant opportunity to search for feebly interacting particles, a field central to understanding dark matter and the matter-antimatter asymmetry, alongside the physics of neutrinos. This endeavor requires both advanced experimental strategies at future LHC runs and solid theoretical frameworks to identify potential candidates for dark matter. This talk reviews ongoing efforts within the LHC to detect new, subtle signatures, focusing specifically on low-mass, weakly decaying particles that emit standard model leptons or appear as displaced vertices.

Language evolution is frequently modeled as a complex interaction between social forces and individual choices. This study examines complex networks where nodes represent individuals, and the links between them are established based on shared linguistic similarity, with edge thickness reflecting the degree of similarity by migration. An existing model, which simulates how languages spread through neighbor imitation without considering movement, is extended to include individual migration patterns, based on the premise that new connections are formed by the people migrants interact with. The proposed method involves first generating a complex network using a specific degree distribution and then adding edge weights to represent migration effects. These weighted networks undergo an iterative pruning process, where edges are removed based on their connectivity; edge probability for any potential link is calculated using a generalized linear model. The main findings indicate that language extinction is more likely in networks with high heterogeneity and that increased migration tends to reduce the number of monolingual clusters. Furthermore, analysis reveals a phase transition in heterogeneous networks, where sudden language loss occurs when migration rates drop below a specific threshold.

This study examines a system of coupled wave equations subject to Kelvin-Vogt damping and a nonlinear frictional force on one subdomain and energy dissipation via a Semilinear damping mechanism on another subdomain. Establishing the well-posedness and deriving optimal energy decay estimates are central to the analysis using Spectral Analysis. The results indicate that in this coupled system, while energy in the region with Semialinear damping decays polynomially at an optimal $\sim 1/t^p$ rate, the undamped portion decays significantly faster at an optimal $\sim t^{-\alpha}$ rate. The study also establishes the stability of the system by proving that the energy decay rate is independent of the domain geometry and the presence of obstacles such as resonances. Finally, the analysis shows that the optimal energy decay estimates hold regardless of the presence of corner singularities in the domain.

The behavior of optimization landscapes is fundamental to understanding machine learning model training. This study investigates the optimization landscapes of concave kernel functions within the overparametrized regime. We demonstrate that, for interpolation conditions, solutions from both Spectral Decomposition (SD) and Gradient Descent (GD) exhibit identical values for the loss, Rademacher complexity, and Spectral norm, with these landscapes becoming locally equivalent around them. Furthermore, we show that for sufficiently early termination of GD, the generated solutions and SD results remain close to each other. Finally, numerical experiments reveal that, for overparametrized settings, employing an overparametrized concave kernel can lead to an improved generalization performance compared to its sharp, smaller-capacity counterpart.

CRESST represents a premier class of experiments in the pursuit of dark matter. Its capability to utilize various crystal-based detectors, each with distinct mass and acoustic and heat detection properties, allows the investigation of a broad spectrum of dark matter particle masses and interactions. In this study, we present the initial results from a combined analysis of data collected by the CRESST-IID and CRESST-III setups. These analyses focus on potential signals from nuclear and electron scatterers caused by incident weakly interacting massive particles. The IIID and III detectors, respectively, employ germanium and lithium fluoride crystals paired with sapphire acoustic sensors. By analyzing germanium-based CRESST-IID data, we constrain interactions with both nuclear and electron scatterers within the sub-GeV to GeV mass range for dark matter. Similarly, lithium-based CRESST-III data allows us to place constraints on the same class of dark matter particles.

Blind image deblurring involves recovering an invisible image from an observation that has been blurred by an unknown kernel. To reconstruct images with superior quality, accurately modeling the unknown blur kernels is essential. In this work, we adopt a kernel mixture framework to represent these unknown kernels and determine their counts using the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Operators. Based on this modeling approach, a novel deblurring framework named FundK mDeblur is established. FundK mDeblur separates mixed kernel structures and reduces complex deblurring tasks into simpler, low-mixture deblurring sub-problems. Furthermore, experiments on various datasets verify the method's effectiveness in performance metrics such as PSNR and structural similarity (SSIM), along with visual outcomes.

Formal verification methodologies enable the integration of rigorous verification into software engineering. Among these, via Hoare logic, we can verify a program's specification using logic and precision. However, current Hoare logic verification tools struggle with two main issues: they fail to account for side effects and lack sufficient automation. To address this gap, this paper introduces a novel calculus, named "Side Hoare Logic," designed to explicitly model side effects. This logic not only enhances the automation of soundness verification but also tightens the correctness guarantees by providing more precise, detailed reasoning about security vulnerabilities.

Distributed databases and blockchains rely heavily on distributed consensus protocols to coordinate behavior among dispersed nodes. However, traditional protocols face a bottleneck by relying on pairwise communication to establish protocol state, which causes them to struggle with high concurrency and scalability. To address these scalability challenges, Canopus, a protocol designed for a stateless network of nodes, is introduced. Canopus ensures stateless consensus by synchronizing the dissemination and acknowledgment of proposals across distributed nodes. The protocol features a unique approach to handling network partitions, ensuring continued progress in scenarios where full connectivity cannot be maintained. The design offers a high level of resilience against network instability and Byzantine faults while maintaining low latency and high throughput even under high concurrency loads. The protocol has been rigorously formalized, with its safety property proven using state machine proof techniques. Furthermore, its liveness property is proven through a constructive proof derived from the protocol algorithm. The practical efficacy of Canopus has been empirically validated through evaluation on both 128-node and 1000-node cloud environments. The results indicate that Canopus can sustain throughput rates exceeding 1000 transactions per second, with a latency of approximately 5 milliseconds, regardless of network scale. The experimental data also confirms the protocol's robustness in maintaining high throughput and safety when a small percentage of nodes exhibit Byzantine behavior or when network partitions occur.

Integrating Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) into robotic systems presents a significant challenge: output uncertainty. This hidden factor complicates the transition from DNN training to real-world deployment by causing unpredictable performance fluctuations due to environmental changes or system degradations like aging components. Current approaches to estimating this uncertainty in DNN regression rely on computationally expensive methods like Bayesian Deep Learning, which are unsuitable for most physical, on-the-ground, and online applications. This research instead tackles classification tasks within robotics by leveraging self-supervised learning (SSL) for fine-tuning pre-trained models using limited labeled data. We introduce a new classification strategy that generates class-specific uncertainty through SSL, effectively mitigting imbalanced dataset issues and enhancing minority class representation. Additionally, by limiting training to highly specific subsets, we achieve higher model accuracy. Crucially, our method is cost-effective and supports real-time uncertainty estimation. Demonstrated through a pre-trained ResNet-50 evaluated on both a handheld scanner and a mobile robot, our findings show that combined uncertainties and specific accurases can serve as reliable feedback for assessing DNN reliability in both online and offline scenarios.

Deep learning models have become standard for traffic forecasting, but they are vulnerable to adversery attacks on both training inputs and test inputs. This paper examines attack scenarios occurring at the inference stage. We show that, with sufficient data accumulation, such attacks remain successful even when limited to very small amounts of compromised test information. To counter this, we propose spatially fragmenting the test area into patches, supplying only some of them to the model. Our experiments indicate that blocking adversaries with insufficient malicious samples of the required critical mass against individual small areas can substantially enhance traffic predictions' integrity and resilience.

In recent years, higher categories have become increasingly relevant in natural language processing, prompting various approaches to their definition. Among these, Gray categories have garnered significant attention for being treated as the primary paradigm of higher categories in NLP, despite the fact that many standard definitions of Gray categories do not align with tricategories. This text demonstrates that by redefining the "associator" within the traditional framework, Gray categories can indeed be equivalent to tricategories defined via weak pseudofunctors. Furthermore, this adjustment clarifies previously confusing notations in NLingst literature, which often obscured the underlying mathematical tricategorical structure by employing ambiguous visual conventions for strict morphisms, 1-morphisms, and associators.

Accurate reconstruction of the hippocampus via segmentation is vital for diagnosing and monitoring neuro-psychiatric conditions. While traditional manual methods remain the gold standard, they are often time-intensive and prone to user error. Conversely, automated deep learning models offer a faster, more reliable alternative but require extensive annotated datasets for training. This paper introduces a new proposal leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to handle hippocampus segmentation. The method begins by utilizing a pre-trained U-Net to generate initial segmentations and probability maps. These outputs facilitate the creation of an edge-weight matrix and an augmented graph capable of learning node embeddings, which subsequently refine the segmentation through three dedicated layers. The network is optimized using the Dice loss function to enhance the overlap between predicted and actual segments. Experimental results indicate that this hybrid U-Net and GNN approach achieves superior performance in preserving hippocampal structure and enhancing overall segmentation accuracy.

We analyze a proposed interferometer experiment claiming a high-fidelity reconstruction of the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state, a setup in which three users navigate a double-slit device independently. However, a critical flaw exists: navigating a two-way path system does not naturally generate GHZ states, as previous research indicates these entangled states require specific multi-level or interaction-driven conditions not met here. To determine if quantum interference truly characterizes the users' movement, we suggest an analytical approach based on calculating the Glickenshield number, a metric sensitive to the presence and nature of multi-parties involvement in multi-part systems rather than just entanglement. By applying this method along with detailed quantifications, we show conclusively that three-body entanglement does not emerge in scenarios involving simple path sharing, reinforcing that true multi-particle correlations and shared path dynamics are distinct phenomena.

This research investigates the generation of inner proton radiation belts by analyzing the time-evolution of proton fluxes at Lagsat, a 1.1 $R_S$ orbiting position, and the simultaneous changes in the solar wind and magnetic field conditions. Data from the PAMELA, Cluster, and the newly installed PAVA instruments were utilized for this study. The study's primary findings indicate that particles likely remain trapped within magnetic reconnection regions in Lagosat's vicinity rather than being directly injected from solar wind disturbances. Specifically, researchers identified three events where proton fluxes increased significantly despite the lack of corresponding solar wind or magnetic field enhancements. During these events, magnetic field measurements revealed a series of reconnection events, suggesting that the magnetic topology in Lagosat's vicinity underwent complex reconfigurations. Furthermore, the study observed an additional event featuring solar wind disturbances and magnetic field enhancements without an increase in proton fluxes. This indicates that not every solar wind or magnetic field perturbation results in trapped particles reaching Lagosat. A correlation was found between proton fluxes and the intensity of magnetic field enhancements within reconnection regions, indicating that particles are likely injected into these regions during reconnection but only become trapped if the local magnetic field topology allows it. The study concludes that magnetic topology changes play a crucial role in the formation of inner proton radiation belts, with magnetic field enhancements serving as a necessary condition for trapping particles.

Deep learning has emerged as a remarkably versatile tool for addressing a broad spectrum of tasks. Expressivity serves as a fundamental limitation in this context, as a network's capacity to approximate a target function determines its maximum potential performance. In this study, we examine expressivity from a practical standpoint, focusing on how model and dataset characteristics influence it. By employing the shuffling paradigm, we demonstrate that both data and network parameters can be leveraged to enhance expressivity. Specifically, we achieve superior outcomes by applying shuffling during training and by incorporating the network's residual across the input and output within its loss function. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks, outperforming current approaches by approximately 0.3% to 1.3%.

We present TrustRegion-Matrix-NN (TR-M-N-N), an innovative architecture designed to facilitate low-rank completion while safeguarding user data privacy. This framework integrates a unique privacy mechanism grounded in an Huber-loss-adjusted trust region approach, ensuring a precise yet robust protection against adversaries who gain access to gradient information. The TR-M-N-N model features both a generator capable of translating noisy observations into clean data and an associated estimator. The former utilizes an adversarial training setup to obscure gradient signals, while the latter employs the Huber-loss trust region to further fortify privacy protection by minimizing gradient leakage. Consequently, the architecture effectively constrains the releaseable gradients to a pre-specified entropy budget. Empirical evaluations indicate that TR-M-N-N surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in real-world applications, achieving a 10% improvement in recovery accuracy and reducing gradient information disclosure by 15%.

We present new high-resolution, high-sensitivity far-IR and submillimeter observations of the star-forming region NGC 2246 utilizing the Herschel Space Observatory's PACS (30--1000 $\mu$m) and SPIRE (350--1000 $\mu$m) instruments. The data reveal extended emission across wavelengths ranging from 30 to 1000 $\mu$m, alongside a point source coinciding with previously identified CO(3-2) emission detected by the ALMA. Analysis of the spectral energy distribution (SED) indicates that the extended emission originates from cold interstellar dust within the molecular cloud, while the SPIRE point source suggests an additional component of warm dust heated by stellar radiation. By fitting radiative transfer models to our SED findings, we derived upper limits for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) abundances in NGC 2446 that fall below standard interstellar levels by one to one-and-a-half orders of magnitude, aligning with established mechanisms regarding PAH destruction in star-forming molecular environments. Consequently, our study offers valuable insights into dust properties within NGC 2446, contributing to the broader understanding of dust evolution in star-forming molecular clouds.

We define a puzzle played on a graph $G$ where, at the start, every vertex has an light illuminated. The goal is to extinguish all these lights. A move consists of selecting a vertex $v$; if $v$ is unchosen, all its neighbors' lights toggle (on becomes off, or off becomes on), but if $v$ is already off, it remains off while its neighbors toggle. We show that for any such resulting state, it is either impossible to reach the all-off configuration or there are many distinct sequences of moves to achieve it. Specifically, either no solution exists, or instead, an exponential number (in terms of $\log_ 2 |E| + O(1)$) of solutions can be found.

Image restoration and image segmentation are two fundamental tasks in image processing. Deep learning approaches have achieved significant progress in both areas. This paper introduces a novel multi-task framework that simultaneously handles restoration and segmentation. Leveraging a U-Net architecture, we adapt the restoration component to function as a multi-scale encoder for segmentation, enabling the segmenter to utilize multi-task training. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive weighting strategy to balance the loss functions of restoration and segmentation. This strategy allows the model to dynamically adjust based on individual image characteristics and tasks, benefiting from both user-defined priors and automatic per-pixel adjustments. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework enables seamless completion of these two tasks while delivering state-of-the-art performance for each individually.

Although the abstract fixpoint phase often generates warnings for non-deterministic programs due to lost loop constraints, existing work suggests that tracing a single execution is insufficient to demonstrate soundness. Instead, this research establishes that one must trace all program executions to verify soundness against the approximations made during the abstract phase. By treating soundness verification as a model-checking problem, we utilize on-the-fly model-checking techniques, analyzing one input at a time. We specifically address scenarios involving infinite traces by utilizing techniques designed for liveness verification. Our approach offers a critical advantage: if one input violates a property, it can be detected without processing additional inputs. We have implemented our method within the KLEE input tracer, evaluating its efficacy against various benchmark inputs.

Outlier detection is a critical component of data analysis, with distance-based methods being particularly prevalent due to their minimal assumptions and extensive real-world utility. Despite recent advancements in the efficiency of bulk-computation distance outlier methods through parallelization, their performance remains constrained by outlier density, requiring significant time to scan the entire dataset in such cases. This paper introduces an algorithm leveraging the GPU's highly parallel architecture to substantially accelerate these distance computations. Additionally, we evaluate various strategies for optimizing these methods on modern GPU architectures and present our contributions as a cohesive suite of CUDA kernels designed for deployment within outlier detection frameworks.

This research investigates the conditions required for excited atomic spontaneous emission to be suppressed when the atom is positioned near a conducting plane. We examine a spin-1/2 Rydbad atom operating within the strong-dipole approximation, parallel to a perfect conductor. In our setup, we analyze how the atom's radiative decay rate varies relative to its isolation in a vacuum. By applying a perfect reflector at a specific minimal distance, we demonstrate that the decay rate can be virtually nullified for any initial excitation $m_i$, representing a significant improvement over the approximate conditions previously identified by Sargent et al. (Phys. Rev. A 52, 5, 6661, 1995), which pertained to $m_i = 1/2$.

Achieving equity in artificial intelligence is increasingly vital, prompting a focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that can learn from graph structures while ensuring fair outcomes. This work introduces a new paradigm known as "neighborhood-level" fairness learning within GNNs. Unlike previous efforts that often sacrifice performance or fail to address specific node group injustices equally, our unsupervised framework enforces that an entire neighborhood's predicted accuracy must align with the average label distribution derived from that same neighborhood's features. Our method integrates with popular aggregation-based GNN architectures through two complementary components: an "induction" mechanism that introduces these local labels during training, and a "regulation" module that applies fairness constraints throughout the process. This framework offers superior flexibility and has been empirically proven to be highly effective on both real-world and synthetic datasets. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies demonstrate that it successfully mitigates algorithmic bias against particular nodes and achieves neighborhood-specific equity.

This paper demonstrates the application of two methods for obtaining analytic approximate solutions of a non-linear reaction equation using a reversible enzymatic reaction as a test case. The first approach is the sub-equations technique, a component of the Karamate expansion method, which yields standard series solutions. To address known issues with this method regarding convergence and stability, the nonlinear adaptive equation method is employed. This second approach is capable of generating both polynomial series and non-series solutions. A comparative evaluation of both approaches indicates that while both provide valid results, each has specific advantages and limitations.

The analysis focuses on the final state characterized by two jets and two missing transverse momenta. The search strategy targets the soft jets originating from the gluino's hadronic decay chain, which serves as a discriminant to identify such events. The sensitivity of the search is defined by the "golden mass" ($M_{\rm golden}$), the largest gluino mass achievable across all possible masses for the final-state particles. At the 100 TeV LHC, the sensitivity reaches a $M_{\mathrm{golden}}$ of 2,800 GeV, probing the entire spectrum of "natural" gluino masses at both 13 and 100 TeV. The sensitivity at 100 TeV is robust against variations in the spectrum's shape, whereas sensitivity decreases significantly at 13 TeV due to the presence of low-momentum jets from the colliding protons. This study introduces a theoretical model grounded in real options theory, designed to mimic the behavior of heterogeneous market participants who exploit financial arbitrage. This group comprises both rational agents, driven by profit, and those influenced by overconfidence, while also accounting for various types of extrinsic financial signals, noise, and inherent uncertainty regarding an asset's fundamental value. Our primary objective is to analyze the conditions under which financial bubbles arise, persist, and burst. To achieve this, we examine the optimal investment strategy for a representative participant seeking anomalous returns via a dynamic programming framework, utilizing a method known as back-and-forth induction. Consequently, we explore the role of individual confidence and the influence of peer sentiment in generating these market anomalies. Our findings indicate that the coexistence of rational agents and overconfident participants, alongside heterogeneous strategies, creates an environment conducive to the formation of self-reinforcing financial bubbles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while bubbles can exist in scenarios involving purely rational participants or overconfident ones alone, mutual interaction with divergent approaches significantly enhances these phenomena.

Recent years have seen significant interest in using recommender systems to forecast ratings within social networks. Although many researchers have aimed to enhance these predictions through various methods, few have specifically sought to leverage the growing volume of user-generated comments. This study introduces a new approach designed to improve rating estimation by incorporating the growing volume of user feedback. It proposes extracting users' comments to perform sentiment analysis, thereby generating as many sentiment scores as possible. These sentiment scores are then integrated into traditional rating prediction techniques to deliver more accurate recommendations. Empirical evidence indicates the proposed method outperforms several established techniques.

Code-switching presents a well-established challenge in linguistics and has recently gained significant attention within natural language processing. However, the complexity of real-world scenarios has complicated research, leading to a concentration primarily on simple, low-code-switch, data-rich environments rather than the dynamic, mixed contexts found in reality. Real-world code-switching is often multilingual and occurs with a high frequency of switches, driving the growth of realistic simulation environments for research. This paper introduces REAL, a comprehensive dataset designed to address these gaps. It features extensive multilingual content with code-switching events across five languages and employs a fine-grained annotation schema to capture recurrence patterns and high-frequency switching dynamics, the latter of which occur over 90% of the time. Furthermore, implementing a comprehensive suite of preprocessing and postprocessing pipelines, we generated over 100 hours of synthetic data by combining REAL with supplementary datasets. Recent years have seen significant development in commonsentence knowledge graphs (CSKG), which compile vast amounts of semantic information essential for natural language understanding. This study introduces an automated approach to unify such concept names using an attention-driven neural framework guided by semantic triplets and external synonym dictionaries. The Hi-GAL initiative utilizes the Herschel satellite to map diffuse dust throughout the Milky Way and nearby galaxies at far-infrared wavelengths of 3.55, 5.8, 25.5, 160, and 350 $\mu$m. This study focuses specifically on the Magellanic Clouds and offers the most comprehensive examination to date of the interplay between various far-infrared bands, combined with optical and near-infrared observations, and the activity levels associated with them across such systems.

Photometric data from the VISTA survey of Redclump giant stars in 11 metallicity-poor globular clusters were used to construct chromosome maps. Although classical Bayes' underpins the standard understanding of cause and effect in physical phenomena, this work demonstrates that it fails in the quantum realm. We establish that the unnormalized posterior probability, rather the proper posterior, serves as the correct underpinning for causality when dealing with quantum systems, diverging from classical expectations. We show that utilizing the classical posterior results in a significant and unbounded quantum risk. To address the associated information processing challenges introduced by the necessity of using the unnormalized posterior, we develop a new framework for quantum decision theory grounded in this concept. Our analysis of specific scenarios, such as simple state discrimination tasks, reveals a novel, nontrivial relationship between the post-update probability (posterior) and intrinsic quantum uncertainty, which is governed by the pre-update probability (prior). Furthermore, we examine the consequences of prior uncertainty within information processing architectures, confirming that classical risk assessments are insufficient and must be extended into the quantum domain.

Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) involves classifying entity mentions into one of hundreds, and often thousands, of specific types. Although pre-trained language models have demonstrated significant potential for this task, their large memory requirements and computational costs often make fine-tuning impractical. To address this limitation, this paper proposes leveraging hyperbolic space to capture the hierarchical nature of FG-NET data. By employing Xformer, a pre-trained large language model optimized for the Riemannian manifold, we successfully lower memory usage and inferential costs. Additionally, because operating in hyperbolic space facilitates efficient type embedding management, we demonstrate the capability to perform this task effectively with an ever-expanding vocabulary of type labels. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves performance comparable to models utilizing Euclidean space.

Cloud data centers (CDCs) have become vital for delivering services to clients. While CDF load balancing is essential for minimizing costs and environmental impact, current methods often fail to fully optimize resources. This paper presents Prepartition, a proactive load balancing method that ensures optimal resource allocation. Unlike traditional techniques that rely on reactive migration of virtual machines to fix over- or under-provisioned resources after they occur, Prepartition uses offline analysis to determine the ideal VM placement and executes the necessary movements online to achieve this configuration. Furthermore, we discuss strategies for handling persistent workloads and offer performance evaluations that demonstrate Prepartition's effectiveness in lowering resource waste.

We present a method for computing an extensive-form game theory model, specifically its Nash equilibrium. In our approach, the input consists of functions representing the agents' evaluation criteria and upper bounds on the maximum achievable value for each agent; these functions are assumed to be continuous and monotonic, but do not necessarily possess closed-form expressions. The output is an extensive-form game where all equilibriums lie within the set of these optimal strategies. Although this concept game may also lack closed-form expressibility, the generated structure is designed to approximate the original agents' functions. We apply our technique to a scenario in computational biology where two agents compete to bind a target protein.

This work addresses the estimation of causal effects when covariates satisfying either the back-door or front-door criteria are partially observed. For such cases, we establish bounds on the causal effects where each bound comprises competing functions reflecting varying degrees of uncertainty regarding the missing data. Assuming missing completely at random (MCAT), these expressions remain tractable and allow for estimation via weighted Sufficient Linkage Rules (SLRs) or similar optimization. We apply this approach in two contexts: first, estimating the total treatment effect when confounders are partially observed under the back-door assumption; second, estimating the average treatment effect on the treated (ETX) when confounders and mediators are partially observed under the front-door assumption.

Attacks targeting Industrial Control Systems (ICS) pose a severe risk to global infrastructure, including power grids, water systems, and manufacturing facilities. The majority of such incidents originate from compromised engineering workstations or technical documentation. Traditional security measures, such as hardware firewalls and network segmentation, often prove ineffective in industrial settings, while relying entirely on system integrity checks is impractical due to the need for frequent system shutdowns. This paper introduces a new approach: a Content Security Policy (CSP) tailored for ICS. This solution enables critical systems to operate securely without requiring shutdowns for integrity verification. We detail the architecture, implementation, and integration of the ICS-CSP, and validate its efficacy through an emulated scenario involving a malicious engineer attempting to disrupt an electric power grid.

Online A/B testing has become a primary method for enterprises operating in digital spaces to evaluate changes in business objectives. The primary challenge for these firms regarding testing efficacy is enhancing average treatment effect (ATE) detection, a goal complicated by the difficulty of accurately defining and estimating the ATE. Research indicates that properly sizing experiments and strategically selecting which tests to run are essential for improving detection, yet current approaches often lack personalization. These traditional methods rely on historical control variance and the assumption of constant effects across all users to determine test value and size. However, in scenarios where outcomes are multifaceted and heterogeneous, this conventional framework becomes insufficient.

To address this limitation, the authors introduce "Variate Selection for A/B Testing" (V4BT), a module designed for enterprise test management systems. V4BT enables enterprises to select specific outcome variables for new experiments to optimize discovery. The system evaluates variables using a two-stage process: first, clustering them based on correlation and variance; second, ranking them based on statistical significance, practical relevance, and clustering similarity. The authors validate the approach through a cloud provider's simulation and a real-world case study, demonstrating that this strategy can increase detection success rates for new features by 10% to 30%.

Software developers often struggle to identify suitable search terms when responding to request-based changes. Entraining—where speakers align their turn-taking in response to one another—is a core component of conversational dynamics. This study introduces a new approach to modeling entrainment that is driven by acoustic features and demonstrates its efficacy in a two-speaker interaction dataset. Research findings reveal a novel link: the probability of entrainment at specific time intervals is positively correlated with the acoustic similarity between speakers at those moments. Furthermore, predicted entrainment probabilities successfully capture key characteristics of real-world events, including temporal evolution, variability, predictive entrainment, and its relationship to speaker dominance.

Subsequently, we validate the approach across three prominent classical convolutional neural networks using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 benchmarks. Results demonstrate that the proposed protocol consistently elevates accuracy, with performance gains that remain robust and independent of network architecture.

We introduce a new fixed-order QCD calculation for the cross section of the neutral-current Drell-Yan process where charged vector bosons decay into the $b\bar{b}$ pair. Utilizing the fixed-order scheme, we organize perturbative contributions systematically across different orders and minimize rapidity-dependent terms at leading order. Consequently, the resulting formulas eliminate the infrared singularity inherent in next-to-leading order calculations performed in conventional factorization schemes and eliminate the reliance on matching coefficients between different schemes. Furthermore, by employing this fixed-order scheme, we demonstrate that rapidity distribution effects remain crucial even at NLO accuracy, and such effects must be incorporated when predicting cross sections and differential distributions at LHC14.

Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as remote vehicles equipped with a steering suit, camera, and speaker, enabling users to travel through various spaces. While the remote QoE is often evaluated in the context of video streaming, the audio-user experience has received far less attention. This study aims to establish a quantitative link between audio packet loss (APL) and the remote QoE for TPoE. To achieve this, the researchers conducted both controlled and real-world experiments across three distinct scenarios, gathering user ratings for packet loss levels ranging from 0.1% to 2%. The resulting data demonstrates a clear correlation between the QoE and APL. Additionally, the findings reveal that the impact of packet loss on QoE is not constant but varies depending on both the specific test scenario and the individual user. The authors also analyzed the relationship between QoE and objective objective measures, specifically Perceptual Evaluation of Audio Quality (PEQOT) and Perceptual Evaluation of Distortion (PED), showing that higher PED and PED scores correlate with improved subjective quality. The results highlight the critical role of adaptive error correction in QoE-driven TPR systems.

Leveraging the flexibility and applicability of Bayesian methods, this paper presents a flexible hierarchical modeling approach for analyzing multivariate count data, featuring overdispersion and incorporating a random effects structure. In this context, the random effects are treated alongside their covariates as latent variables within explicit hierarchical frameworks. Analyzed through a Bayesian regression setup, the relationships between these effects and covariates are assessed via a precise model selection technique utilizing information criteria alongside Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques implemented via reversible jump MCMC. Using bacterial count data from an agricultural experiment, the study demonstrates how this framework can model complex, data-driven patterns and flexibly handle diverse scenarios.

The electrical conductivity of nanomaterials hinges critically on their carrier mobility, a factor profoundly shaped by interactions with phonons. Investigating these phonon–carrier dynamics necessitates a thorough grasp of phonon dispersion alongside spatial variations in conductivity across the material's surface. In this study, we introduce a novel technique utilizing a scanning superconducting quantum interference device (scanning SQUID) to map surface conductivity changes caused by phonon scattering during carrier excitation events. Specifically, this approach captures phonon–carrier signals through alterations in local conductivity's coherence across the material. Experimental findings reveal distinct phonon scattering effects at room temperature in both In$_{0.03}$Ga$_{0.97}$As and graphene. These observations, corroborated by standard measurements of thermoelectric and photoluminescence responses, validate the viability of scanning SQUID for elucidating nanoscale phonon–carrier mechanisms.

Intended to address clustering issues in multi-feature high-dimensional data, this work develops an innovative ensemble framework. By recognizing that not all features hold equal importance for specific data points, the authors introduce a flexible algorithm capable of assigning variable weights to features, with the parameters of this initial method grounded in Mean Shift clustering. Furthermore, the study presents a second complementary algorithm based on K-Means clustering to ensure a robust hybrid approach. These distinct algorithms are subsequently integrated using weighted ensemble techniques. Experimental outcomes indicate that this Hybrid Ensemble Weighted K-Means (HEWK) framework surpasses existing solutions in solving complex clustering problems.

Although quantum gravity is anticipated to explicitly break all global symmetries, their theoretical utility remains significant in particle physics and cosmology. This paper demonstrates that even if such symmetries are violated, their associated Nambu-Goldstone bosons (GBPs) can still emerge, provided the violation is extremely slight. In this scenario, a highly populated background state enables these GBPs to exist; however, this environment results in them lacking "natural" stability against explicit breaking terms. We demonstrate that this instability takes the form of a partial decay into massless Standard Model particles. This finding suggests that future experiments searching for NGBPs might detect evidence of these global symmetries from fundamental physics frameworks.

We present photometric data from the globular cluster NGC 1846, featuring a blue straggler star (BSSt) located in the cluster's outer regions. This system is unique as a binary composed of two BSSt-mass stars that form a wide orbit. The presence of such a distant binary challenges standard two-body dynamical evolution models for blue horizontal branch stars, which typically predict rapid destruction via stellar encounters. Instead, these findings support dynamical evolution models that attribute horizontal branch star formation to interactions within a dense stellar environment. Consequently, if this BSST originated from dynamical evolution, this discovery offers a compelling case study for future investigations. Photographic observations of this cluster were conducted using the 1.2-meter telescope at Las Campanas Observatory.

The success of transferring pre-trained models has transformed the deep learning field, enabling researchers to build on existing knowledge for new tasks. However, transferring a pre-trained model to a downstream task is not always successful, and understanding why remains a significant challenge. We posit that the limited transferability stems from a conflict between the knowledge encoded in pre-trained models and the requirements of the new task. Specifically, knowledge acquired during the pre-training phase can create "inherent biases" that negatively impact downstream performance. To address this, we present a new approach called Knowledge Forgetting and Unlearning (KFU). This method applies a forgetting strategy to mitigate the influence of these inherent biases. We demonstrate that our proposed KFU framework significantly enhances the transferability of pre-trained models across diverse downstream tasks.

In numerous complex systems characterized by interdependent nodes, information spreads along various pathways. While prior literature has extensively analyzed how network structures affect diffusion performance, it largely overlooks the impact of partitioning methods on these assessments. To address this gap, we introduce a unified evaluation framework for information efficiency in complex networks, examining results across four distinct partitioning strategies. Our findings demonstrate that modularity-based partitioning outperforms homogeneous, hierarchical, and other approaches. Furthermore, modularity not only accelerates overall information propagation but also enables the modular optimization of this spread process. Consequently, modularity serves as an essential criterion for evaluating and comparing efficiency in complex network information propagation.

A primary challenge in detecting Android malware is that adversaries can easily modify existing samples through simple, strategic alterations, rendering them harmless to detection systems; this attack vector is known as problem-space evasion. While recent studies have attempted to counter these issues, they frequently fail because the alterations made to evade classification occur in a manner that is not fully predictable or controllable during the classification process itself, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose *Attack Space Search*, a novel approach utilizing search algorithms to construct evasion sequences that are short yet highly effective. Specifically, we apply Beam Search to evolve malicious applications capable of successfully deceving ML models with minimal changes. Evaluation on two leading public Android datasets demonstrates that Attack Space Search achieves superior results compared to current state-of-the-art evasion techniques. Code and associated data are available at https://github.com/AndroidMalwareDetection/Attacks_Space_Search.

While prior theoretical work attributed this effect to a $- \frac{1}{4}\pi$ Pfaffian state (representing only half a quantum), we demonstrate here that within the thermal QHE framework, such features can instead signal half-integer quanta arising from a fully defined particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological phase. A definitive method to resolve this ambiguity involves analyzing the temperature dependence of the thermal Hall conductivity to determine the precise state. We have established that both hypotheses can be validated experimentally and provide distinct, predictable functional behaviors, while also offering new insights into the physical origins of these conductive signals.

We demonstrate that forming Thakurta black holes—a specific type hypothesized to constitute both the seeds of present-day black holes and dark matter—requires an immense energy scale within the range of $10^{31}-10^{32}$ GeV. Given these constraints, the necessary physical conditions for this mechanism remain unlikely to occur throughout our universe.

Protoplanetary discs frequently exhibit pressure maxima, which facilitate the formation of spindly structures resembling the co-planar co-spinning stripes seen in HL Tau 55 and HP Bop by aiding pebble core accretion at typical spacing. This study investigates how pressure bumps influence the internal dynamics, chemical composition, and evolutionary pathways of disc systems, utilizing a novel disc model that accounts for both hydrodynamics and the transport of energy and matter. Our simulations reveal that pressure bumps can trigger localized hydrodynamical instabilities, resulting in distinct stripes of enhanced density that evolve over time. Furthermore, these structures influence the transport of heat and chemical tracers within the disc, altering its chemical fingerprint. By tracing the migration of these stripes over extended periods, we provide insights into long-term disc evolution and its impact on planet formation outcomes.

Overparameterization has emerged as a pivotal phenomenon in machine learning, enabling the successful learning of tasks even with model architectures that far exceed parameter counts necessary from a functional standpoint. Tradistically, this surplus is viewed as a practical workaround to bypass combinatorial challenges inherent in standard gradient descent local minima, necessitating a functional equivalence between deeper models and simpler shallow networks. In this paper, we reframe overparameterization through the lens of computational complexity, moving away from minimization dynamics. Our findings establish a functional and operational correlation between overparameterization and the concept of overcomputation. Specifically, we demonstrate that within a functional and training-time invariant framework, agents capable of learning tasks successfully require computational operations that substantially surpass the minimum theoretical bounds required. We further illustrate that overparameterization serves as a fundamental constraint of computation, deriving this constraint from generic properties related to compressibility and the lengths associated with programs and data.

Ridepooling has emerged as an effective strategy to encourage the shift from private car usage to car-sharing within urban settings. However, providers face a complex challenge: simultaneously maximizing passenger detour minimization and pooling rates. To address this, the authors introduce a new method for designing optimal ridepooling routes that incorporates this dual objective. Since the resulting routing problem is complex (NP-hard), the authors propose two efficient parallelized heuristic algorithms. Testing the approach using datasets from New York City, London, and Paris demonstrates its superior capability over competing heuristics in balancing detour minimization and high pooling rates.

Multi-Modal Fusion (MMF) in E-Commerce presents significant hurdles, primarily due to the need for data alignment and issues arising from imbalanced or missing multi-modal data. To address these challenges, we introduce the Non-Linear MMF (NL-MMF) model designed to execute these tasks through a streamlined, single-stage architecture. This DL-based framework features a specialized Non-Linear Cross-Modal Attention (NCMA) module capable of dynamically reorienting focus toward specific regions in imbalanced scenarios while effectively fusing cross-modal information regardless of input volume. Additionally, an innovative Non-Linear Region Decoder (NRD) has been developed to further enhance performance. Experimental outcomes confirm the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

Deep InfoMax (DIM) represents a specialized deep learning framework designed to leverage shared information across multiple instances of input data. This approach successfully identifies correlations between disparate modalities, spatial locations, or temporal moments. Recently, DIM has been widely adopted in brain imaging for tasks such as detecting neurodegeneration and characterizing Alzheimer's disease. Current DIM implementations typically rely on a linear transformation to align feature distributions, a strategy often insufficient when distributions are non-Gaussian. Addressing this limitation, this study introduces Deep InfoMax with Kernel (DIM-Kernel), which substitutes the traditional linear layer with a Gaussian kernel to compute exact kernel space alignments. By utilizing the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), this method enables accurate distribution alignment regardless of statistical distribution. Experimental evaluations on two public datasets demonstrate that DIM-Kernel consistently outperforms existing DIM variants and prevailing models in DIM-based analysis tasks for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. The comprehensive source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/AlzCoop/DIM-Kernel}.

Obtaining a deep comprehension of textual data is a vital yet difficult challenge in natural language processing. Addressing this, our research introduces an original influence score (I-score) designed to quantify the relevance of every token within a text classification framework. By measuring how much a token contributes to shifting model predictions as it moves from the input to the output, I-score provides an efficient, fully-differentiable mechanism that functions within the end-to-end knowledge discovery process. Through extensive experiments on various text classification datasets, we demonstrate that I-score facilitates obtaining significant insights into model decision-making without compromising accuracy; in fact, when applied together with standard feature selection protocols, it further boosts classification performance.

While numerous metrics exist to estimate the test error of AI devices using distribution shift models, current methods typically evaluate performance in isolation and fail to identify the factors that lead to failure. To address this, we present a comprehensive approach for interpreting AI medical device errors, specifically designed for image-based classification tasks. This method integrates established metrics with Shapley values to generate an interpretable assessment of device performance. By combining the robust quantification found in the "Deep Learning for Healthcare" framework with our interpretative solution, this approach provides a complete view of AI medical device performance assessment. We validate this method using two real-world datasets: the RIMone breast cancer screening dataset and the MIM-CAC-180 collection.

Duda's Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) serves as a theoretically lossless entropy coder achieving the Shannon limit, operating on a forward model with reversible precision via a backward pass. While this tANS method boasts constant, albeit imperfectly quantified, overhead, our analysis demonstrates that reverse indexing can be eliminated by applying the inverse function cyclically to initial table states. We evaluate this strategy using a 10 MB "sophisticated" test file and three initial states: the identity matrix, a state resulting from Duda's exact initialization repeated 2^32 times, and a state from repeated applications 2^32 + 10 MB of data. Our findings show a 0.14-bit redundancy deficit for tANS when using the initial state derived from Duda's initialization, compared to the standard 0.15-bit redundancy in the original algorithm. However, this advantage disappears with the other conditions; the table state produced by repeating the precise initialization 2^32 + 10 MB of data yields performance matching Duda's initialization, incurring the same 0.15-bit redundancy.

The dielectric behavior of liquid electrolytes encompasses complex phenomena arising from both intramolecular and intermolecular ion interactions. Using molecular dynamics simulations combined with classical electrostatics, we examine the dielectric properties of aqueous lithium chloride across varying concentrations. Our findings indicate that while intramolecular contributions from water and the small number of ions are minimal, intermolecular interactions between ions play a significant role in determining the dielectric response of the entire electrolyte system.

Pedestrian trajectory prediction is a critical technology with applications in human-robot interaction, autonomous driving, and safety surveillance. Current deep learning-based approaches, however, often fail to accurately forecast trajectories in the presence of occlusions and complex, unpredictable real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, this study proposes a new framework, TrajNet, which employs contrastive learning to predict future paths. The model features two interconnected subnetworks: a feature extraction component that generates encoded trajectory representations, and a prediction subnetwork that forecasts future trajectories from these features. By optimizing the system through contrastive learning—specifically by maximizing the similarity between synchronized features of adjacent frames—TrajNet produces more accurate and robust results. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets and experimental conditions confirm the model's superiority. The findings demonstrate that TrajNet significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10.8% improvement in occluded scenarios and a 5.6% improvement in open scenarios.

We introduce a novel statistical method designed to quantify the Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) activity within the nearby universe. Our approach evaluates the spatial distribution of 1,666 X-ray AGNs from the 1RXF-VEGAS catalog, situated within 60 Mpc of Earth, against 1,666 random positions drawn from an astrometric model. These random samples account for the inhomogeneous spatial density of host galaxies by incorporating morphological classifications—specifically elliptical, spiral, and irregular types—based on the Petrosky radius. By analyzing the morphological types surrounding "random" locations to map the expected spatial distribution, we establish a baseline for AGN-host galaxy associations. We then compare this expected distribution with the actual spatial profiles around each individual AGN to determine if their local environments differ significantly from chance projections.

Nuclear short-range correlations (SRCs) in light nuclei are known to elevate their kinetic energy, yet it remains uncertain whether this kinetic energy boost persists when many-nucleon systems are packaged within a nucleus. This study investigates many-nucleon subsystems inside deuteron and the $^3$He using quantum Monte Carlo methods to examine this question. Our analysis of wave function data reveals that a significant portion of this added kinetic energy manifests as high-momentum nucleons contained within nucleonic subsystems. Specifically, we compute the energy density matrix for two- and three-nucleon configurations, which allows us to quantify the fraction of elevated kinetic energy found inside these specific subsystems.

We introduce Complex-Valued Convolutional Neural Networks (CvCNNs), extending convolutional networks with complex numbers to the full depth and width of a neural architecture. We further develop complex-optimized regularizers, including one based on the entropy of the output distribution to enhance learning efficiency, and adapt the popular ResNet architecture to operate effectively with complex numbers. Evaluating our approach across three standard image classification benchmarks—CIFAR-10, STLMN, and TNB (ImageNet)—demonstrates that these models achieve superior performance, surpassing existing real-valued baselines in accuracy.

Epidemic dynamics are frequently simulated using complex network structures to represent interactions among individuals, with standard simulation methods relying on $N$ sequential steps, where $N$ denotes the total population size. We introduce a novel approach for epidemic simulations by partitioning individuals into clusters, thereby reducing execution time to $M$ steps, where $M$ represents the minimal count of clusters. We provide the theoretical basis of our method through the development of a new clustering algorithm. We define the concept of "cluster distance," which facilitates the simplification of contact patterns within and across clusters by summarizing them into distance metrics. We then introduce a simplified optimization problem to identify optimal cluster distances that closely approximate the original contact data while significantly streamlining the propagation process. We demonstrate that our cluster-based SI model performs excellently even with minimal clusters, maintaining high accuracy relative to the standard model while offering substantial time savings. We validate these findings using both synthetic networks and authentic contact data derived from the COVID-17 pandemic. We anticipate that our framework will enable a broader adoption of complex network theory in the epidemiology sector.

In CMB map-making, maximum likelihood estimators are frequently employed to derive instrument maps from data, though they are known to be sensitive to model errors stemming from unaccounted nonlinearity, time-varying parameters, or neglected forward model aspects. The primary contribution of this work involves establishing an asymptotic upper bound on the loss of local efficiency experienced by the true ML estimator when a specific model error exists yet is omitted from the algorithm. By leveraging the relationship between local efficiency and the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), the authors derive and implement a two-time-scale stochastic approximation algorithm capable of computing the FIM for large time sequences, which subsequently facilitates efficient calculation of the efficiency bound. Numerical evaluations indicate that the proposed efficiency estimation method is substantially faster than traditional Monte-Carlo techniques.

Instructing a system to execute actions, such as making and consume snacks, often involves verbal commands like "grab the chocolate and eat it." However, if multiple objects share the same visual appearance and multiple people are present, ambiguity may arise, hindering the teacher's intent and causing learning errors. To resolve this, we investigate the utility of establishing a shared common ground, which we posit can effectively disambiguate references. We posit that the interaction between a teaching agent and an executing machine can be effectively modeled as a game of semantic text generation, where both the output and environment are constrained to ensure coherence. Our findings, supported by experimental data, indicate that generating statements which accurately reflect the shared context significantly aids the performer in identifying the correct objects.

Quantum process tomography is a fundamental capability for developing quantum computers and quantum networks, as well as a key enabler for highly sensitive quantum metrology. However, the difficulty of current methods scales exponentially with the number of qubits. This study demonstrates a single-shot method for characterizing quantum processes that overcomes these limitations by requiring resources scaling only polynomially with qubit count. Achieving this efficiency depends on utilizing a highly entangled probe state prepared in a specific single-shot manner; this is most readily done with clusters of trapped ions. Furthermore, we illustrate how full process information can be extracted from a subset of accessible two-qubit correlations. Finally, it is shown that the precision of this single-shot characterization converges to the performance achieved with traditional multi-shot strategies.

This paper investigates the attainment of tight bounds on the Cheeger constant within the realm of convex geometry. Specifically, it establishes sharp bounds derived from natural geometric measures, including perimeter, area, and diameter. Additionally, it presents two families of convex shapes that serve as examples to demonstrate the tightness of these theoretical limits; notably, the findings extend to any setting where the triangle inequality holds.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer a promising solution for delivering wireless access in regions where network coverage is sparse or infrastructure is inadequate. This study introduces a novel approach to optimize the power transmission levels and three-dimensional flight paths of an UAV, designed to boost the signal strength at the distant edge of coverage while the drone hovers over the area. This optimization challenge is addressed efficiently using a Lambda-based algorithm. This method rephrases the core problem as a constrained maximization task for a function that depends on a single variable: the Lambda. By applying a well-established convex optimization technique known as dual decomposition, the researchers can derive the precise global maximum. Finally, the performance of this proposed algorithm is verified through comparisons with other standard methods.

The Internet of Things (IoT) facilitates the interaction of diverse smart gadgets within the cloud by exchanging data over the internet. As IoT devices are often deployed in public spaces, the transmission of information between them and the cloud creates significant security and privacy challenges. To protect data in transit, conventional encryption algorithms are widely utilized; however, their heavy computational demands and high power consumption make them unsuitable for resource-constrained low-powered devices. In response, this research introduces a lightweight encryption technique tailored specifically for IoT architectures.

Spin qubits are emerging among the leading technologies for advancing fundamental physics research, particularly in precision measurements involving light and matter interactions. However, current spin qubit detection methods often lack sufficient efficiency, primarily due to the time-consuming nature of Ramsey measurements. This limitation can be addressed by truncating Ramsey sequences at an optimal, pre-determined point. This article introduces an algorithm to automatically calculate this truncation time by maximizing the measurement efficiency for each individual spin qubit. The algorithm's efficacy was validated through numerical simulations and experiments conducted on transmon-qubit interfaces utilizing two different types of readout configurations, demonstrating a high success rate in optimizing both single and dual readout methods.

Centrality metrics are typically used to assess a node's potential influence within a network. While methods like degree centrality focus on immediate neighbors and eigenvector centrality considers influence throughout the entire network, these approaches often overlook how influences spread through indirect, multi-hop connections. This paper focuses on networks characterized by triangle inequality excess (TIE), where shortest path lengths between indirect neighbors exceed the sum of individual paths. We propose Gromov centrality, a refined version of Geodesic (shortest-path) centrality that specifically addresses networks with significant TIE. Unlike standard centrality measures that neglect the impact of negative triangles and TIE on influence diffusion, our method offers a novel perspective. We demonstrate that in networks with high excess TIE, Gromov centrality converges to either standard degree centrality or PageRank centrality, depending on the specific structural characteristics. Additionally, we show that for a broad category of networks, Gromov centrality shares the same ranking order as Geodesic centrality. These findings suggest that our new centrality framework offers a refined and superior approach to analyzing networks with substantial TIE.

B. N. Parlett, in his book on symmetric and nonsymmetric eigenvalue problems, discusses transforming matrix pencils into the Kronecker canonical form via a similarity transformation. The Kronecker canonical form consolidates into block upper triangular structures all essential information regarding a matrix pencil's characteristics, including its eigenvalues, right eigenvectors, and both right and left minimal kernels. However, the specific methodology Parlett describes relies on strategies from symmetric eigenproblems, requiring transformations that maintain both symmetry in the constituent blocks and the overall block structure. Since this requirement necessitates both block symmetry and block sparsity preservation, the classical approach is unsuitable for the vast domain of problem areas involving block sparse symmetric matrix pencils. In the present work, we present modifications of Parlett's original algorithm that achieve simultaneously the Kronecker canonical form and the Kronecker normal form. These updated methods retain the block structure and automatically yield block symmetries in the resulting blocks, all without ever explicitly computing either the matrix's factorizations or its eigenvectors. In summary, our new procedures are efficient, scalable, and capable of handling large-scale problems.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis seeks to determine sentiment polarity toward specific aspects within product reviews. This paper presents a hybrid optimization framework for maximizing information sharing in RIS-assisted ISAC systems, which simultaneously serve radar and communication tasks. In relativistic quantum field theory, an inertial observer perceives Minkowski space as vacuum, yet the field's modes observed by an accelerating observer appear populated with particles. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the phenomenon is not confined to the mode-counting argument but applies to every aspect of quantum theory that relies upon light-cone structures.

The resulting 36-tight features were quantified as a ratio of feature flux to the magnitude of the primary galaxy's flux. This low chance level confirms that the high occurrence of bright features around massive galaxies is unlikely to be intrinsic; instead, they likely stem from recent accretion events or interactions within the last Gyr.

Additionally, our findings reveal a strong correlation between parameter-level forgetting and conventional techniques for evaluating the success of continual learning methods.

While recent advancements in hardware have helped mitigate computational and data processing bottlenecks at the source, quantized neural networks continue to offer substantial efficiency gains in terms of storage and computation. Additionally, these models exhibit robust performance despite noise and lack the need for specialized high-end hardware to run. However, maintaining model accuracy during the networking process remains a significant hurdle. This paper addresses the critical task of preserving performance in quantized neural networks by utilizing a multi-objective optimization approach. We propose a method that automatically determines the optimal bit-width for both weights and activations based on a specific accuracy and computational budget. By formulating quantization as a constrained, multi-objective optimization problem, our method delivers superior model performance with reduced parameter size and lower computational load. Experimental results across various image classification datasets confirm that our approach achieves a notable balance between accuracy and efficiency.

Continuum soft robots offer great promise for complex tasks within both biological and industrial environments. Nevertheless, inherent difficulties such as strong coupling between joints, inherent nonlinear dynamics, and signal noise impede precise and reproducible control. Recent advances in deep learning have shown potential to address these challenges, though existing methodologies often rely on supervised learning using externally tagged forces or require extensive prior knowledge of the system, thereby limiting their practical application. This study introduces a self-sensing framework for continuum robots that leverages a unsupervised learning approach to identify nonlinear dynamics directly, eliminating the need for external load cells or pre-defined models. Crucially, this method enhances control accuracy under noisy conditions by filtering out inherent measurement noise from the actuators, relying only on deflection data from the robot itself for identification. Validated through both simulations and physical experiments, this adaptive control scheme facilitates a broader deployment of precise, self-aware driving strategies in self-monitoring robots.

The real Jacobi group ${\rm Sp}(2,\mathbb{R}}$ contains a structure as a semi-direct product of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R}}$ and the Heisenberg group ${\rm Heis}(\mathbb{R}}$ acting on the real plane. In previous work, we defined a discrete subgroup $\Gamma$ within G^J(ℝ) consisting of elements with specific entries and provided its geometric presentation. This paper focuses on the structure of Gamma 's normal subgroup H, which is defined as the kernel of Gamma 's homomorphism mapping to SL(2,Z). We demonstrate that H corresponds to the center of Gamma and is entirely comprised of points on the center of Gamma. This result implies that H forms an infinite-index Heisenberg subgroup. Furthermore, we establish the existence of H's complement in Gamma, which is isomorphic to the center of Gamma. This paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings and their potential applications in the field of geometry.

Verifying facts using structured data is difficult because statements often include language that does not directly align with schema elements. To address this, we introduce a data augmentation method for an exact matching checker that converts natural language queries into equivalent forms using available structural data. Our approach includes (a) techniques for identifying relevant table columns and (b) techniques for generating relevant statements from that data. We evaluate our method using two datasets containing table data and corresponding search results. Our results demonstrate significant performance gains, achieving an F1-score of 6.7% improvement over state-of-the-art results. Bayesian differentially evolution (DE) algorithms, such as the stochastic optimizer known as DE, have gained popularity in high-dimension inference tasks, particularly within machine learning. In this study, we investigate the DE method from the standpoint of non-identifiable statistical models. Using mathematical techniques, we demonstrate that, when applied to DE, the generated Markov chain converges to the target posterior distribution. This result is achieved by employing an acceptance/rejection rule to generate proposals from the current distribution and then applying them according to certain criteria. Our findings show that the DE method, under appropriate conditions, converges to the target posterior distribution by generating proposals from the current distribution and applying them through an acceptance/rejection rule that satisfies specific criteria.

We examine the issue of fault-tolerant distance labeling within undirected graphs, where the objective is to assign concise labels to each vertex that enable the computation of vertex-to-vertex distances even if up to $f$ vertex labels are obscured. While prior research primarily addresses this problem for constant values of $f$, we propose a novel algorithm suitable for polynomial $f$, specifically where $f = O(n^{1/(1+L)})$ and $L \geq 1$ is a parameter governing the label size. Our method produces labels of length at most $O(L \cdot f^{L/(l+1)})$ and performs in $O(f^{L/(l+1)})$ time and space, covering the previously studied cases of $f$ as a constant or the entire setting for all pairwise distances. We further demonstrate that our approach serves as an optimal solution previously established by Han et al. for maintaining shortest paths in dynamic graphs involving both vertex and edge deletions.

We examine the time evolution of quantum many-body systems characterized by a finite Liouvillian gap $\Delta_{\rm gap}$ and relaxation time $\tau_{\rm gap} = 1/\Delta_{\rm gap}$, which are defined as the real part of the Liouvillian eigenvalue closest to the stationary state. The study focuses on spin-1/2 lattice models at the integrable point via exact numerical solutions, specifically analyzing pure spin-wave initial conditions. At the non-interactable limit, the real component of a frequency-specific two-particle correlation eigenvalue, denoted as $\Omega_k$, was calculated. A pronounced secondary peak was identified within the imaginary part of this value, occurring at $2\omega_{k}^0$, where $\omega_k^0$ represents the magnon dispersion relation. This same secondary peak appears in the correlation function's imaginary spectrum. Consequently, these results demonstrate that two-particle correlations exhibit oscillations at twice the magnation frequency, suggesting that higher-order oscillations corresponding to $N\omega_k$ (where $N$ approaches infinity) are predicted to exist.
