Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is vital for the safety and dependability of automated systems, a need particularly acute in medical imaging. This study addresses OOD detection for slice-level tasks in CT and MR scans using a contrastive learning framework. Our approach maximizes intra-class similarity while minimizing inter-class interaction from normal and OOD data, ensuring these representations remain distinct. We evaluated our method across three novel test sets: the LiSSR dataset for single-source domain adaptation, the LiSSR-MultiSource for multi-source domain adaptation, and the LiSSR-MR for magnetic resonance images. Comprehensive results demonstrate that our strategy effectively identifies out-of-domain and out-localization aberrations.

We examine a two-level system driven by periodic forces while remaining open to investigation. When this quantum system is coupled to a thermal bath, a steady state emerges as the limit where time approaches infinity. The position of this steady state in the Bloch sphere fluctuates periodically, matching the drive's period, yet its spherical orientation remains invariant. In contrast, for a bath composed solely of bosons, the system reaches a distinct steady state as time goes on to infinity. This final state traces a specific linear trajectory on the Bloch sphere that remains independent of continuous driving, simply rotating on the plane aligned with the oscillation frequency. These theoretical predictions are backed by results from experiments conducted on trapped ions.

This study examines the convex solution $u$ of the Monge–Ampère equation with zero boundary conditions, demonstrating that the Alexandrov maximum principle implies $ \alpha $-H\"older continuity where the exponent $\alpha$ corresponds to the solution's convexity at the boundary points. These findings extend previous results by J.S. Jel\"ynek, S. Lu, and S. Wang, encompassing a broader spectrum of conditions regarding convexity at the domain's boundaries. Furthermore, the discussion outlines additional constraints necessary to secure the sharp $ \alpha $-H\"older continuity based on the assumption of boundary convexity for the solution.

Time measurement relies on comparing a periodic signal with a stochastic clicking process at the reference; this approach has been underutilized in clock design. This paper re-evaluates the fundamental comparison between the spectral domain, contrasting periodic oscillators against clickers (discrete events). It examines how operating within the spectral domain affects this comparison and derives the optimal filtering strategy to achieve the minimum variance in time interval measurements. This optimal variance formula applies universally across any oscillator type. The ideal low-pass filter characteristics are derived for both continuous models and specific technologies: continuous clickers (Poisson processes) and standard types including mode-locked lasers, single-photon detectors, and tunnel diodes. Theoretically, this optimal variance scales with the average energy transmitted during each click. Consequently, the performance of these clickers is benchmarked against periodic signals with equivalent energy parameters. The analysis concludes by proposing an improved time-interval detection method that integrates the principles of this optimal filtering.

This paper presents a unified approach to integrating Software Defined Networks (SDN) with Fog computing, targeting enhanced resource management, streamlined multi-tier coordination, and improved Quality of Service. To achieve this, we developed TFOG, a distributed framework capable of deploying, monitoring, and managing SDN controllers within an optimal地理位置 (geographical location). The underlying methodology employs distributed graph algorithms to identify and deploy the necessary number of controllers across the most suitable locations to guarantee optimal network performance. Furthermore, we implemented a novel algorithm designed for distributed graph isomorphism detection to verify that network topologies remain consistent across various controller instances. Additionally, we suggest an algorithm for identifying isomorphic subgraphs within a network. The practical viability and effectiveness of our proposed TFOG framework were validated through a real-world deployment on a substantial network infrastructure.

Pair-wise loss facilitates metric learning by optimizing embeddings to ensure image representations from identical categories are closer together, while those from different categories are pushed further apart. In offline applications like image search and retrieval, the approach typically involves two stages: embedding learning and building an embedding index. However, in dynamic scenarios where new categories or samples continuously emerge, maintaining this index becomes challenging. A newly appearing category or sample requires embedding retraining and the subsequent update of retrieval indices, which creates significant computational overhead. This study proposes a novel image retrieval framework that addresses these dynamic challenges without necessitating full retraining. The core of the solution is the $Delta$-Deep-Index (D-DI) model, which leverages the newly acquired data to update existing embeddings via a dedicated $Delta$ network. This model is specific to new categories or samples and is independent of the primary deep network. By utilizing the newly acquired image pairs, D-DI $updates$ the $Delta$ network and effectively updates the global image index through the combination of pre-trained embeddings and these specialized networks. Experimental evaluations on the Pascal VOC retrieval dataset confirm that the proposed model updates faster than existing methods and achieves superior performance.

We demonstrate that a broad class of these quantum holographic tensors exhibits a robust capacity for quantum error correction, accompanied by a related recovery process. This feature stems from the tensor network's geometric properties, which also serve as the foundation for the dual Chernov-Zilinsker theorems. Leveraging a specific form of quantum error correction, we derive the error correction codes realized through holographic tensors, as well as the associated quantum recovery maps. Furthermore, we show that the boundary region's entropy changes under error applications to a bulk state follow a holographic pattern that replicates the generalized entropy formula defined in quantum gravity.

This study investigates the magnetic architectures of clustered, magnetized radio filaments located in the Galactic center region, utilizing novel data from the upgraded Galactic Plane Survey (GPS) in association with existing data from the VLA Galactic Plane Survey (VGPS). We identified 11 clusters ranging from 10 to 100 kiloparsecs in size, each containing numerous magnetized radio filaments identified via VGPS. Most filaments exhibit significant polarization, with typical values around 10% and an average length of 1.5 parsecs. The clusters display a variety of macroscopic morphologies, including linear, branched, elliptical, and network-like structures. Our analysis reveals that filament orientations within each group are generally consistent on scales of 10 kiloparsecs but exhibit random or complex patterns at smaller scales of 100 to 1000 astronomical units. Furthermore, the relative polarization angles between filaments within the same cluster generally fail to show coherent trends, lacking consistent patterns at intermediate scales of 1000 to 10000 astronomical units. These outcomes strongly indicate that although related radio filaments within a cluster are influenced by a common large-scale physical mechanism, their local orientations result from complex local dynamics.

This study examines Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) and Voltage Sensitivity (VS) within high/medium-voltage layered distribution systems, presenting a novel approach to modeling these aspects across different voltage levels. The proposed method represents each three-phase feeder as a cascade of equivalent networks and applies them sequentially to construct an equivalent model of the entire YG/M/V system. Furthermore, a specific formulation is developed to account for the voltage sensitivity of the distribution system. Finally, a new formulation for the CVR problem is developed, which integrates a new high-voltage section model and incorporates the VS metric.

We introduce a new approach for the general case of nonstochastic bandits and experts involving delays in both feedback to the algorithm and to the environment. By utilizing memory-efficient exponential weighting combined with potential-based analysis techniques, we demonstrate an inherent balance between feedback delay (F) and environmental delay (E). Specifically, when both types of delays are positive, our approach yields regret bounds of $\tilde{O}((F+1)(E+1)\sqrt{T})$ for full feedback and $\tilde{O((F+1)^2(E+1)\sqrt{T}})$ for the partial arm feedback case. Furthermore, we provide matching lower bounds for these nonstochastic settings. In contrast to a recent non-probabilistic paper on online linear optimization by Li and Yuan (2023) which did not account for environmental delays in its main contributions, our analysis explicitly incorporates F and E into the non-probabilistic framework.

In task-oriented dialogue, dialogue models trained via reinforcement learning often exacerbate lexical degeneracy, where repeated outputs like a single word or its variants are repeatedly generated. This phenomenon arises because these models effectively minimize entropy maximization errors, a tendency that can be mitigated by designing reward mechanisms that penalize low diversity. This work is the first to empirically examine how enhancing rewards for diverse outputs influences the generation capabilities of task-driven conversation models. Specifically, it evaluates how this reward-based approach performs in the challenging BAbI task suite. Results indicate a trade-off between using diversity-based rewards and other metrics: while a model optimized solely for diversity may yield diminished task accuracy, incorporating a diversity component within the reinforcement learning framework can achieve scores comparable to models that prioritize other objectives exclusively.

The unpredictable nature of the 2-on-1-step load responses generated by three-bladed offshore wind turbines (OWT) exhibits heteroscedasticity, which significantly hinders accurate prediction accuracy. This heterogeneity arises from varying turbine operating conditions and environmental stochasticity. This paper introduces a data-driven framework designed to model these non-stationary load responses by integrating a state-based approach with Kernel Hilbert Space (KHS) operators. The framework utilizes a state derived from the Online Principal Component Analysis (OPC) of load time-series to capture evolution, while employing Operator Kernel Ridge Regression (OKRREG) based on features extracted via online Principal Component Analysis (Principal Component of Loads) to adapt the model in real-time. The study evaluates this novel method against a traditional benchmark, Linear Regression (LR), utilizing KHS operators. The comparison focuses on prediction accuracy, computational efficiency, and the model's adaptability to evolving operating conditions. This paper presents a new approach to identifying low-quality text generated on social media during events like the 2020 Beirut explosion. Our proposed method is a new deep neural network architecture called Multi-Head Attention Network (M-ANN), designed to detect spam and malicious posts. The system takes unstructured text as input and outputs a probability score indicating how likely the text is spam or malicious. We evaluated our model against existing state-of-the-art methods for detecting spam and malicious posts on social media, finding significant improvements in accuracy. In addition to these performance gains, we also analyzed the computational efficiency of M-ANN compared to these existing methods, finding that M-ANN has lower memory requirements and faster training times.

This study introduces SceNDD, a naturalistic driving dataset focused on scenarios, which captures data from both the vehicle interior and exterior over a period of 12 hours across three days. The recorded information includes vehicle dynamics, driver behaviors, traffic context, and environment information, all synchronized with the vehicle's CAN bus data. Built upon a comprehensive data processing pipeline, the dataset includes preprocessed files optimized for research, specifically tailored to support the development of new methods in road safety and driving tasks.

In this article, we extend boundary conformal field theory concepts and entanglement wedge geometry within higher-dimensional setups. Specifically, we generalize reflected entropy and its associated area law for entanglement wedge cross sections, allowing arbitrary configurations of intervals and slits. This generalization finds roots in universal laws of entanglement entropy around singularities and around isolated regions. Furthermore, we derive universal behaviors for entanglement entropy near isolated islands and examine their geometric counterparts through modified Wilson loop relations in gauge theories.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) offer a promising approach to enhancing wireless communications by creating controllable propagation environments. In this study, we examine RIS-assisted orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (RIS-aided OFDM) systems, where the reflection coefficients across RIS elements are adjusted to maximize the received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) under an isotropic distribution constraint without element phase noise, alongside a realistic model that accounts for phase noise at each element. Two methods for mitigating phase noise in the metasurface are analyzed: element grouping and optimized subcarrier mapping. Corresponding optimization formulations for maximizing SNR under these phase noise constraints are established. Numerical results confirm the methods' effectiveness in overcoming phase noise impacts and demonstrate the performance gains of the proposed SRT schemes relative to standard schemes.

This study analyzes a specific type of weak quantum measurement designed to optimally acquire coarse energy measurements. By defining the quality of such a measurement as the average fidelity of an energy state prior to undergoing unitary evolution, the paper identifies the optimal strategies for minimal disturbance. Our findings indicate that the precision of the energy levels measured is the critical factor, more so than the coupling strength of the meter; notably, even high-precision meters can induce significant disturbances in quantum states.

The COVID-19 pandemic has spurred the development of numerous digital contact tracing applications across the United States. Despite widespread adoption, these apps face significant privacy hurdles that threaten their scalability. This paper presents a privacy-enhancing workflow grounded in homomorphic encryption to enable secure, real-time contact tracing with minimal computational overhead on encrypted data. By employing this approach, app developers can launch a fully functional system without compromising user confidentiality. Our advanced architecture enables users to generate access keys that allow their devices to compute proximity alerts against nearby users' devices— all while keeping individual identities and personal data hidden. This process is executed directly on the device, eliminating the need to send sensitive information to a central server. Furthermore, this encrypted protocol is compatible with various tracing architectures, including centralized, decentralized, and the Google Apple framework.

This study examines privacy and PIN management within Signal through surveys, polls, and targeted interviews involving 150 participants across 30 generational cohorts. We uncover significant disparities in how users approach PIN enthusiasm versus casual signal management; notably, active signal enthusiasts often prioritize account accessibility over privacy, whereas casual users may inadvertently compromise their privacy in pursuit of better accessibility. To address this, we highlight critical gaps in Signal's PIN privacy features and propose concrete recommendations to enhance PIN management architecture, availability, privacy standards, user education, and empirical research within this platform.

Natural languages often mark grammatical gender on nouns, a feature that indicates sex or class information. In many cases, noun embedding models successfully transfer this gender distinction into their vector representations; however, it remains uncertain whether these representations accurately capture the semantic significance of that gender. This study demonstrates in a series of analyses, specifically examining a vast corpus of English text representing four distinct gender categories, that inanimate nouns consistently project meaningful gender distinctions in their embedded vectors. We validate this finding by showing increased co-occurrence frequencies for nouns sharing the same gender and by successfully training classifiers to predict the gender of inanimate nouns based solely on their vector representations. These results indicate that standard word training data inadvertently captures nuanced gender semantics for inanimate objects—a phenomenon of significance given the contested nature of gender among both humans and non-human entities.

In this article, we investigate stiffness within the context of measure-theoretic entropy for non-stationary probability measures. Our primary findings present a unified framework that connects various classes of dynamical systems exhibiting non-stationary behavior, characterized by hardness or inertial properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that Lebesgue measures on minimal one-dimensional systems with completely homogeneous entropies, smooth measures on a rigid system, and specific finite Borel probability measures on the one-shift all exhibit non-stationary stiffness. Additionally, we provide an example of non-stationary hard space, a finding that extends a result from the work of Bouslimani and Climenhaga (2019). The paper also includes supplementary material related to non-stationary ergodic theory.

Although pose estimation for novel object categories remains a significant challenge, recent research has made notable progress in this area. ZOPe leverages an object alignment network (AN) trained on the dense functional body part (DFBP) representation, where body parts are defined based on dense functional relationships. This process results in the generation of DFBP representations. Finally, ZOPe utilizes a Displacement Field Regression (DFR) module that takes both the global image context and the DFBP representations to calculate precise pose estimations. Accurately forecasting traffic conditions is essential for many traffic management applications. This study introduces an ensemble model that combines multiple deep learning algorithms with differentiable non-numeric features, specifically incorporating spatial adjacency and temporal lag. By utilizing a gradient boosting framework, the system processes these feature-rich inputs to generate short-term traffic state predictions. The model's performance is benchmarked against several standalone deep learning models using real-world datasets, consistently demonstrating prediction accuracy gains of approximately 3% to 5% across various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, ablation studies indicate a robust enhancement in performance by integrating multiple feature types, though the advantages are somewhat less pronounced when considering temporal features in isolation.

This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed to infer causal structures and identify confounders from multivariate data. Our approach utilizes a Structurally Causal Model (SCM) grounded in a specific causal graph. We formulate the problem as a variational inference task, optimizing both the SCM's parameters and a graph-based structural prior. To optimize this hierarchical probabilistic model, we develop a variational objective that can be maximized using standard gradient methods. We analyze VACA's capacity for causal learning, particularly regarding its identification of confounders, through synthetic datasets simistic confounding scenarios. Additionally, we evaluate the method using a real-world, highly confounded temperature dataset. Our results demonstrate that VACA successfully recovers causal relationships and the hidden confounder, outperforming existing variational models which fail to accurately detect confounders.

The two dominant paradigms for vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (VCLIR) are the pointwise approach, which maps queries and documents to equivalent vector spaces, and the pairwise method, which translates similarity scores between items using domain adaptation techniques. Although the pointwise framework has gained popularity, it faces limitations: achieving high performance requires extensive, fine-grained training data, and it struggles to effectively model complex query-document relationships. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces Pairwise Analogical Extention (PAME), a novel approach that adapts pairwise similarity into the CLIR context using vector analogical reasoning rather than direct mapping. Specifically, PAME extends these operations across multiple dimensions to capture intricate associations between queries and documents. Evaluations on three large-scale English-Chinese cross-lingual retrieval datasets demonstrate that PAME achieves significant improvements in both unsupervised and weakly-supervised scenarios outperforming the analogical pointwise method.

Pruning techniques have proven highly effective at shrinking the substantial network sizes produced by contemporary deep learning architectures. A long-standing challenge in computing the anomalous dimensions associated with multi-leg operators to very high loop orders is the extreme proliferation of contributing diagrams. This difficulty is particularly acute when evaluating contributions from bulk terms in the four-loop anomalous dimensions of four-parton operators; previous studies by various groups have reached results extending to ten loops, a process necessitating the enumeration of over 100,000 diagrams. In this study, we streamline the computation by restricting the operator content to those with five or more legs, where the scaling of loop orders is significantly reduced. Specifically, analyzing these multi-leg operators ensures that only the leading singularity arising from infrared regions contributes to the calculation. This insight allows us to express the operator's anomalous dimension as a differential integral equation featuring integrands that consist of compact combinations of compact-loop functions. We validate this methodology by computing the leading-order contributions to the anomalous dimensions for five and higher leg five-parton operators up to the six-loop level. Our findings demonstrate excellent agreement with determinations of total (soft plus bulk) anomalous dimensions derived by the Collaborations for Precision Phenomenology (Collab. for Precision Phenomenology) to six loops, which had previously required a diagrammatic summation spanning more than 100,000 configurations.

For the Visual Domain Adaptation (VADa) challenge 2022, a task involving automatic semantic segmentation, we developed an approach centered on Entropy Minimization. In this framework, the model generates synthetic training examples by cropping them from the target domain to assign pseudo-labels based on the model's current high-confidence predictions. Following their generation, these labeled examples are utilized for self-training to refine the model. Additionally, we incorporated the Backprop Domain Bottling (BBD) technique, which optimizes the feature extractor in the target domain through backpropagation, thereby enhancing the quality of extracted features and improving performance. Our method achieved the second-best overall ranking in the VADa 2022 competition, attaining a mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) of 42.07% and ranking first among all deep learning-based approaches.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a widely adopted algorithm for reducing high-dimensional data to fewer dimensions, operating by modeling local data relationships through a Gaussian distribution and approximating their pairwise distances in lower-dimensional output via a heavy-tailed Student's t-distribution. While effective for visualization, this approach frequently lacks the quantitative reliability necessary for downstream tasks. This limitation stems from dual sources: first, Gaussian's assumption of short student distances often results in overcrowding, completely distorting global data structures; second, the algorithm's greedy optimization strategy, typically solved using gradient descent, can get trapped in local minima, preventing an accurate representation of all stochastic pairwise distances. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a non-Gaussian deep generative model capable of accurately capturing both long-range and short-range interactions. Our approach employs explicit $\ell_p$-norms and $\ell_0$-norms to promote sparsity and long-tail characteristics, enabling more precise low-dimensional learning. Extensive experiments across various benchmark datasets confirm that our proposed method surpasses traditional t-SNE in achieving more accurate representations and maintains superior numerical stability during downstream applications.

This study explores an alternative derivation of the Hitchin connection defined on the moduli space of marked $\overline{D}_g$ curves. Additionally, it validates our conjecture concerning the specific form of this connection.

The global pandemic has driven a widespread shift to working from home, creating a unique challenge for organizations and their staff. Addressing employees' psychological needs is crucial for their overall well-being and organizational resilience. This study utilizes Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to examine these specific needs within the remote working context, based on survey data collected from 266 employees in Spain. The findings indicate a significant autonomous motivation among the participants, yet they reveal an unexpected low ranking for perceived perceived relatedness. This result highlights the difficulty of maintaining a sense of belonging and connection when working remotely. Consequently, these results call for strategic adjustments in how managers support their teams to ensure psychological needs are met in an effective remote environment.

Dichotomous matrices play a pivotal role in controlling the dynamics of linear differential equations defined on the real axis. While every dichotomous matrix within the space of $n\times n$ real matrices possesses an essentially Hermitian counterpart, this property does not necessarily hold when elements are drawn from the Gaussian integers, $\mathbb{Z}[i]$. This distinction raises critical questions regarding the matrix exponent's spectrum and Riccati theory over $\mathbb{Z}[i]$. This paper addresses these issues by establishing conditions that ensure every dichotomous path in $\GL(n,\mathbb{Z}[i])$ admits an essential Hermitian generator.

Using the ALICE detector at the LHC, this work presents measurements of the azimuthal asymmetry, $p$-dependence of beauty-hadron decay electrons ($R_{p}^{2}$) in heavy-ion collisions. These data provide insights into how beauty quarks interact within the dense quark-gluon plasma generated during heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the study examines nuclear modification factors of beauty-hadron $R_{p}^{2}$ transverse momentum dependence and elliptic flow. Positive trends indicate beauty quarks traverse the plasma without experiencing significant drag forces, while the elliptic flow suggests they undergo weak coupling interactions within the medium.

Inspired by Michael Hutchinson research on the fundamental distinction between the chromatic numbers of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the authors introduce chromatic sets and define them as the smallest range of distances required to color any finite set of points in Euclidean space, \(\mathbb{R}^n\), such that no two same-colored points are separated by a distance within that interval. This research, examining how these values are determined for dimensions \(2\) through \(8\), confirms that the exact chromatic set is achievable for every case studied, thereby resolving a question posed by Paul Erd\H{o}s, Gerhard Nagy, and William Schaffer.

This paper addresses the problem of gain calculations for the maximum entropy (or extremal) gain in finite, infinite networks without drift, focusing on scenarios where users are independent but not necessarily identical. Specifically, under independence assumptions, characterizes the asymptotic behavior as the count of users tends toward infinity. This asymptotic behavior can be determined by optimizing a zero-input zero-output process across the user ensemble. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that the maximum entropy (or extremal) gain in finite, infinite networks without drift, as determined asymptotically when user numbers tend toward infinity, exhibits linear dependence proportional to the user population. The associated optimal zero-input zero-output process for this asymptotic extremal user gain exhibits a specific structure: it is constructed by superimposing independent but not necessarily identical zero-input zero-output processes for each individual user.

Methodologies for categorizing large-scale datasets are increasingly vital in auditing, particularly as the need for transparent, non-explainable categorization grows. We introduce a new approach that applies the Simpson rule to a non-explainable machine learning model to derive explainable categories. We evaluate this framework using commercial software where training data was developed by a team of auditing experts. Results demonstrate significant improvements in predictive performance and reveal that the standard Simpson rule application may produce overly complex explanations. To address this, we propose two new interpretative techniques that generate more effective results.

The STrauss process is a point process characterized by a constant interaction density among points separated by a specific distance. While this model can represent phenomena such as long-range repulsion and short-range clustering, its parameters have never been reliably estimated from data. This study addresses that gap by introducing robust methods for estimating the parameters of the STrauss process using data from simulated experiments. While the proposed methods are validated on synthetic data, their practical utility in analyzing real-world point pattern data is demonstrated and discussed.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), emerging from string theory and quantum gravity, implies a fundamental minimum length alongside standard quantum mechanics. While the GUP's gravitational origin suggests deformations in the commutation relations of position and momentum, most prior research has overlooked its potential impact on the gravitational field itself. This study aims to investigate the relationship between the GUP and quantum gravity within the framework of canonical loop quantum gravity. A key challenge in this analysis is that current GUP formulations are insufficient for quantum gravity integration, necessitating a new framework: the GUP-based Hamiltonian approach. Utilizing this method, the authors re-evaluate black hole thermodynamics and derive a novel deformed path integral measure for the Schwarzschild metric.

This paper addresses multitasking scheduling for systems utilizing functional units with distinct capabilities. In this framework, each task comprises a set of functions, some of which can execute on multiple types of hardware, while others are restricted to a single unit. The goal is to create an optimal schedule that minimizes makespan while ensuring all dependencies are met. Although the problem is proven to be NP-hard, we present an algorithm based on branch-and-bound that effectively solves it for moderate instances. Additionally, we introduce the concept of "critical functions"—those whose processing time directly dictates the optimal makespan—along with corresponding bounding techniques that significantly enhance search efficiency. The paper also defines "marginal tasks," which represent the subset of tasks most likely to determine the makespan. By focusing the initial branching sequence on these marginal tasks, we can substantially reduce the total number of required branches. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully solves instances with up to 20 tasks within a reasonable timeframe.

Navigating deformable terrains poses significant challenges for legged locomotion due to the complex, unconstrained nature of these surfaces. While recent years have seen progress in both modeling and controlling such systems, performance remains limited by the difficulty of analyzing these terrains and selecting appropriate gait strategies. This paper introduces a novel, data-driven approach to robotic walking on deformable ground using learning-enhanced, contact-rich dynamics. Our methodology relies on a flexible, input-driven dynamical model that incorporates dense sensor data, including inertial measurement unit (IMU) readings and outputs from an electrical muscle-based actuator. This model enables rapid computation of torque and contact forces within the leg, as well as the reaction forces exerted on the terrain, facilitating robust and agile navigation even under uncertain conditions. Specifically, we employ recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to regulate RIMPET (a legged robot equipped with artificial muscles) across various deformable landscapes. Experimental results confirm that the robot maintains stability while traversing these unstable surfaces, demonstrating superior resilience to both ground and internal reaction force perturbations.

This study details the performance of a 4G LTE cellular network, operated by Orange S.A. and optimized for Machine-to-Machine (M2M) and Internet of Things (IoT) services. The research focuses specifically on a 4G network deployed in the 700 MHz spectrum within the 12th arrondissement of Paris. This infrastructure supports a deployment of 125 dual-mode (4G/LTE-IoT and 4G/LTE-Advanced) base stations designed to serve dual purposes: supporting traditional LTE-Advanced services for standard mobile devices and supporting LTE-Advanced IoT services for machine communication. These services facilitate a wide range of applications and are critical to Orange's strategic vision for its B2B2C IoT portfolio. To evaluate the network's Quality-of-Service (QoS) under real-world conditions during firmware updates, the authors utilized drive tests to collect KPIs. A key objective was to determine if these firmware changes introduced any degradation in service. The findings indicate that network performance improved following these software upgrades. Furthermore, the authors have demonstrated that standard KPIs are insufficient for a comprehensive evaluation and that a proposed novel framework for measuring QoS is necessary to properly capture the nuances of IoT network performance.

We evaluate the local fock-space self-energy across the many-body localized (MBL) regime of the disordered fermionic fermi-liquid model using auxiliary fields. This approach allows us to demonstrate that, given sufficient disorder, both the local Fock-space self-energy and the single-particle self-energy remain bounded. Notably, the imaginary component of the local Fock-space self-energy serves as a direct proxy for determining the decay rate of an initially localized state. Our analysis further reveals that while disorder growth increases this self-energy's magnitude, while while the impact of weak interactions is relatively limited. These outcomes underscore the viability of an auxiliary-field framework for studying many-body localized phase characteristics within larger, more intricate systems.

Conformance checking focuses on reconciling recorded behavior derived from event logs against a modeled process definition. Alignments represent a cutting-edge technique for identifying, locating, and quantifying deviations in process executions, working alongside case studies to analyze individual traces or groups of alignments to evaluate different recorded executions. While alignment methods are currently a popular research topic, they are not yet integrated into standard conformance checking software. This paper introduces "pyalign," an open-source Python library that facilitates the computation of various alignment types. We discuss the design and implementation of "pyalign," and also its usage for conformance checking and case study analysis under differing conditions.

In this paper, our focus is twofold: examining the benefits and limitations of both analytical and empirical radio propagation models, as well as deriving a new empirical model to account for propagation around the 59 GHz frequency band in urban settings. We categorize radio propagation models into two distinct groups. The first comprises analytical models, which begin with physical wave principles, apply simplifying approximations, and yield closed-form equations. The second category includes empirical models derived from experimental data fitting to determine model parameters. While analytical models offer the advantage of scalability across different environments without the need for additional calibration data—a feature particularly beneficial for network planning—they often require extensive calculations and produce less precise outcomes than empirical counterparts. Conversely, empirical models deliver greater accuracy but demand a substantial dataset for training and recalibration when applied to different scenarios. To address these limitations, our novel approach utilizes a data-driven methodology. We collected measured signal measurements from various frequencies around 60 GHz in an urban area and employed a nonlinear regression technique using a complex-valued Gaussian function. This function incorporates a decaying exponential of a term derived from a complex Gaussian distribution, allowing it to account for free-space path loss, multipath fading, and the complex nature of antenna radiation. Our findings indicate that the proposed model delivers a fitting precision comparable to full-wave simulations without incurring the significant computational costs associated with analytical models.

This study investigates power system model (PSM) sensitivity using models of varying orders, physical energy-based metrics, and computational energy-based measures. Results indicate that model error grows exponentially with increasing network distance from the event origin point. Both energy-based metric types identified the highest-sensitivity PSMs as those lacking sufficient dynamic representation in areas closest to the disturbance. We propose a computational energy-based measure (CEBM) that aligns with human perception and effectively quantifies transient stability across events. A recommended strategy for selecting optimal model reduction levels involves choosing the PSM with moderate sensitivity that exhibits similar transient outcomes to the high-order version. Ultimately, CEBM offers a means to assess sensitivity across different scenarios and guides the selection of appropriate model orders for specific applications.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for both the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems under boundary conditions within an open, bounded space. Specifically, we consider Dirichlet, Neumann, or no-slip flux types for Poisson's equation and either bounded or elastic scattering boundaries for the Vlasov component. The validity of these results relies on a key spectral condition for the 20th century elastic case. Finally, we demonstrate that these solutions converge toward continuous smooth steady-state solutions of the full system.

Software development routinely involves processing large volumes of natural language text within requirements, bug reports, and other documentation to handle change requests. However, developers often struggle to interpret these requests due to their linguistic complexity, which can require significant manual effort to locate relevant sections in code. Consequently, there is a critical need for automated tools to facilitate software maintenance tasks. This study focuses on developing such a system to automatically identify the specific lines of code affected by a change request. The approach begins by locating a set of relevant files based on request keywords and then applies customized state-of-the-art machine learning models to detect altered functions, classes, and modifications within them to estimate the impact of the change request. Validating this methodology on two change request datasets yielded promising outcomes, demonstrating that the system successfully located relevant files with precision of 0.8098 and F1-score of 0.5948 for identifying altered software components, achieving a combined precision of 0.8098 and F1-score of 0.8098.

Colloidal gels are 3D networks of particles held together by weak, face-to-face particle-to-bond interactions that exhibit viscoelasticity and a yield stress. In this work, we investigate the rheology of such a system subjected to ultrasonic vibrations. By applying controlled ultrasonic energy, we demonstrate the ability to modulate the gel's viscoelastic characteristics and yield stress across the full spectrum from ultrasonic frequencies down to zero shear rate. Specifically, we observe a transition from a viscous fluid state at high ultrasonic activity levels to a rigid elastic solid regime at low activity. This behavior transitions through a distinct peak in both the storage ($G'$) and loss ($G''$) moduli as a function of vibrational activity. Furthermore, during a low-frequency rheo-acoustic transition monitored in a frequency sweep, a characteristic hysteretic loop emerges at the critical point where the solid-liquid switch occurs at low-frequency shear rates. These empirical findings are supported by a theoretical framework that attributes these shifts to the reversible breaking and reforming of particle bonds induced by vibrations. Ultimately, our observations confirm that shear-induced structural changes in colloidal networks can be directed by external vibrational forces, opening avenues for new strategies in designing functional materials.

This paper introduces a variant of the classic stable marriage algorithm, named short preference lists (SPL), which relies on priority assignments within each group of candidates rather than individual complete lists. SPL is computationally efficient, requiring only linear time relative to the total number of candidates across all lists. This efficiency makes SPL particularly well-suited for large-scale short preference lists. We demonstrate SPL's applicability in two domains: assigning students to schools and in cloud computing infrastructure, specifically regarding the provisioning of redundant resources for fault tolerance. In the context of school admission, SPL outperforms the standard algorithm by significantly improving the average preference rank of students who are matched. In cloud computing, the redundancy required for maintaining system reliability introduces new matching challenges. We address this by adapting SPL to form a short-redundancy stable matching that pairs both primary and secondary resources, with SPL's time efficiency remaining intact.

Summary evaluation is challenging due to extensive and intricate human annotation requirements. Current automated summary evaluation metrics often fail to capture the nuanced qualities perceived by human evaluators. This study investigates SummScore, a novel metric that measures summary quality across four dimensions: semantic, structural, stylistic coverage, and summarization. We conduct an empirical analysis using human-rated machine-generated and rephraseable summaries. Our analysis reveals that SummScore effectively captures stylistic and structural dimensions often neglected by existing metrics. We also analyze the performance of various large language models (LLMs) in auto-evaluating summaries and observe that these models can consistently apply SummScore criteria. Their performance suggests that models can successfully evaluate summaries using automated systems, offering promising insights into the future of summary evaluation.

Two distinct regimes are analyzed: first, a static initial condition where convection arises, followed by second a standing wave setup where the laser is already established. In both cases, a heat transfer model coupled with convolution equations derived from fluid fluid dynamics and Maxwell's energy conservation laws is developed. These dynamics equations incorporate two mechanisms for the moving fluid to interact with the laser: direct self-focusing (where light follows the temperature gradient) and stationary light absorption within the fluid.

The results indicate that laser self-focusing is significantly influenced by the pre-existing temperature distribution generated through heat transfer. Furthermore, when stationary light absorption is included, both light self-focusing and the energy transfer process become highly non-linear. The study concludes that while laser energy propagation and the resulting liquid flow can be effectively controlled through heat transfer, the degree of this control is constrained by the specific parameters of the absorbing medium, such as the magnitude of the absorption coefficient.

Determining the quality of output for academic authors and institutions is a critical yet intricate endeavor. This is further compounded by authors frequently publishing across various institutions during the movement involved in collaborations and post assignments. This work introduces "venue scores," a metric designed to assess the quality of academic venues while accounting for differences in the intrinsic quality levels distinct between conferences and journals. Our methodology for utilizing these venue scores relies on Value the Web Ranking (WebRank) to adjust for publication quality. Learning-based methodologies are increasingly recognized as critical components in modern control systems; however, the dependence of these algorithms on neural networks creates a challenge, as neural networks are difficult to analyze for safety properties. While prior research has examined boundability by proving robustness or demonstrating non-robustness, the actual violation of a specific system when a network fails is often not directly established. In this paper, we present two new methods to certify robustness directly within a single-step or multi-step framework, specifically tailored for feedforward and recurrent neural networks. We also provide counter-examples that illustrate the non-robustness of these systems. In comparison to prior studies, our approach is more computationally efficient and can be used to directly identify specific network inputs that cause robustness failures. Additionally, we present a theoretical analysis of the relationship between the network's architecture and robustness.

This paper examines established theories rooted in dissimilarity-based clustering, drawing inspiration from three primary domains: a) the science of classifying patterns, b) multivariate analysis, and c) graph theory. Tensor completion focuses on recovering high-order random matrices from sparse observations; it has become a vital tool in computer vision and graphics for tasks like view synthesis, shape reconstruction, and surface rendering. While prior research has achieved notable success, many existing methods are computationally prohibitive for large-scale applications due to slow convergence rates and high computational costs. To address these limitations, this study introduces an enhanced large-scale tensor completion framework built on a new sparse modeling approach, the Sparse Tripartite Graph (STG). Specifically, we propose the STG as a tripartite graph encompassing visual data, a semantic graph, and a three-dimensional modality matrix, which facilitates the joint modeling of inter-view, inter-modality, and intra-modal correlations. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm leveraging the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to enable rapid and scalable tensor completion across massive datasets. Empirical evaluations on both standard benchmarks and extensive large-scale datasets confirm that our approach achieves superior performance with significantly accelerated training speeds.

Heavy flavor hadron and jet measurements are essential for understanding parton distribution functions (PDF) in the $x$ range of 0.1 to 0.3, a critical region for understanding proton structure at the LHC. This update addresses the so-called "proton size problem," an issue where previous global fits struggled to reconcile certain electroweak and parity-violating electron scattering observations. Incorporating temporal information into knowledge graph embeddings (TKEs) has proven beneficial for downstream tasks like temporal relation prediction and entity alignment. Nevertheless, numerous real-world knowledge bases include event facts involving a start and end date, possessing an explicit temporal scope. Existing TKE approaches largely ignore this scope, potentially leading to performance degradation. This study introduces a new model, STKE, designed to effectively integrate temporal scopes into the TKE framework. Our approach extends the conventional logic formulation used in TKEs by constructing a generalized constraint structure capable of representing both the temporal scope of facts and the relationships between time intervals. Additionally, we develop a specific loss function aimed at enhancing the discrimination power of embeddings linked to time intervals during training. Experimental results demonstrate that STKE surpasses current state-of-the-art TKE models in terms of the distinctiveness and clustering characteristics of generated embeddings, yielding improved performance on temporal entity and relation prediction tasks alike.

Ultrashort pulses from ring-mode locking lasers achieve high peak power through self-phase modulation and pulse-pair formation, which demand sophisticated geometric analysis. This study leverages the $\Lambda$ (lambda)-map, a standard tool for normal-dispersion fiber amplifiers, to accurately model the ring-resonator layout. Applying this framework, the authors derive the condition for passive mode-locking initiation, analyze the dynamics of the pulse and pulse-pair shapes, and identify the optimal point of self-phase modulation that yields the sharpest pulse duration. Additionally, the framework connects the magnitude of pulse power within the gain medium to the gain bandwidth, driving the most brief pulse width at the output.

Federated learning (FL) presents a promising approach to machine learning, offering valuable data privacy benefits. Experimental results indicate a notable improvement compared to existing methods. The challenge of creating unlimited synthetic data for a given scene is crucial for advancing computer vision and remote sensing. While current methods rely on natural image priors to perform inductive extrapolation from new scenes, most are constrained by a narrow training dataset. This approach achieves superior high-fidelity results due to its robust handling of high-variance image features and a focus on realistic scene synthesis. Complex networks are frequently modeled using systems with stochastic nonlinear dynamics, which can display randomness that significantly impacts their functional output. This study presents a methodology for constructing such networks based on complex oscillatory networks. The approach involves mapping these underlying simple systems into corresponding complex dynamical nodes, where each connection corresponds to synchronization between oscillators. The mapping process is governed by a deterministic chaotic system, specifically the Lorenz model. The resulting network is characterized as a stochastic dynamical system where Lorenz trajectories determine the structural topology and intrinsic stochasticity, while external noise influences its functional operation. The research analyzes dynamical behaviors across varying noise levels and demonstrates that amplifying network robustness entails sacrificing functional flexibility. Furthermore, it establishes that networks built from complex oscillatory cores are capable of maintaining operational functionality even when their structural topology is severely disrupted.

We investigate temporal Lipschitz stability of time-continuous $\alpha$-dissipative solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation, where $\alpha \equiv$ a constant belonging to the interval $[0,1]$. Specifically, by defining dissipation and negative (or positive) Hessian forms, these solutions are characterized as those trajectories that can be constructed by solving a specific system of ordinary differential equations—driven by a dissipation parameter and governed by the respective geometric structure—starting from any given initial condition. We demonstrate that for any such permissible initial condition, neighboring trajectories evolve in a way that is globally Lipschitz controlled over time by their initial distance of separation. This establishes that all $\alpha$-dissipative solutions enjoy intrinsic Lipschitz stability.

Collected during robotic ultrasound procedures, scol curvature measurements offer greater precision, efficiency, and reproducibility compared to their manual counterparts. This study introduces a deep learning approach that trains a neural network directly on robotic ultrasound video frames to estimate the scol curvature angle. The method utilizes the inherent structure of the spinal column to generate keypoint landmarks along its curve. These inferred point clouds subsequently serve as input for a polynomial regression algorithm designed to estimate the curvature angle. We evaluated this deep learning framework against two baseline approaches previously assessed in the scol research domain across different data sets. Experiments demonstrated that both our proposed method and the updated baseline that incorporated our proposed keypoint generation and regression architecture achieved superior performance on the spinal curvature estimation.

This study introduces a novel framework for modeling duration in text-to-speech synthesis. We analyze two primary training objectives: modeling both the median and the mean of duration distributions. While the median can be represented by the median of aligned duration values from speech corpora using a single static constant, the mean typically requires an end-to-end learning approach. By employing a multi-task learning architecture that leverages a median-prediction subnetwork to aid mean-prediction, we successfully utilize a single subnetwork for both. We further propose a novel regularized cross-entropy function for the median-prediction subnetwork to enhance its stability and performance. Experimental outcomes indicate that employing the median yields superior synthesis quality and more robust results compared to using the mean.

Specifically, by transforming standard argument extraction tasks into a maximum dependency parsing problem, our approach efficiently extracts triplets from large-scale text corpora. We demonstrate that these algorithmically generated triplets are of high quality and can effectively guide state-of-the-art extractive models. Multi-input multi-output (MiMiO) architectures are highly efficient for modeling problems with both spatial and temporal dimensions, effectively decomposing a 3D problem into two 1.5D components. Our findings indicate that MiMiO models fail to leverage all available parameters, with the extent of underutilization scaling with the model's spatial field of view (SFOV). To resolve this, we introduce a new class of SFD- aware MiMiO architectures that adapt the spatial field of view dynamically rather than using a fixed size, thereby fully exploiting capacity without increasing model depth. Empirical results across image classification and classification tasks confirm that these new architectures match top-performing existing architectures while reducing their parameter counts by up to 2.3x.

This research investigates the detection of hate speech in Hindi and Bengali, aiming to develop robust models that leverage data augmentation and ensembling. Detecting the directional nature of nuclear recoil events is a highly desirable outcome for both dark matter detection and neutrino research. Over the last few decades, numerous experiments have been developed to achieve this goal. However, the most recent efforts, such as the SuperNEMO project, demand a large number of two-dimensional (2D) gas-proportional position-sensitive detectors, each requiring a precise, uniform high voltage supply. SuperNEMO will utilize a vast array of ~1000 such detectors, prompting a search for a solution that can interface with them, deliver 100% 2D coverage. Additionally, the system must be non-metallic to prevent interference with the magnetic field of nearby muon coils during the facility's initial phase, which involves studying the neutrino oscillation mechanism at intense muon beams. Commercial driving requires decision-making that is deeply influenced by its unique contextual factors, such as driving environment, operational policies, and driver-specific traits. While current learning and inference models often rely on data-driven approaches, they frequently fail to fully capture all relevant contextual variables due to data scarcity and estimation difficulties, which can negatively impact road safety. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a context-aware model leveraging knowledge graphs (KGs) to model the complex interconnections between drivers, operations, and the road networks. Utilizing the flexibility and composability of KGs, this model can effectively integrate diverse data sources and explicitly represent dense networks of contextual elements and their mutual relationships. The study introduces new data schemas and specific structural features for modeling drivers, operations, and driving environments, then embeds them within a unified KG framework. Furthermore, this model redefines the concept of a "context" as a subgraph of the knowledge graph and introduces corresponding metrics to quantify similarity and relevance between drivers, operations, and environments. Experimental results indicate that this model outperforms alternative methods regarding both the accuracy of inferences and safety metrics for commercial driving environments.

Computed Tomography (CT) has become a standard diagnostic tool in medicine, yet scanning procedures are often optimized for speed rather than image quality. While this prioritization leads to motion artefacts, it also causes beam-hardening artefacts when polyenergetic X-ray sources interact with varying tissue densities. By reconstructing these idealized, artefact-free coefficients via Total Variation (TV) minimization using sparsely sampled noisy X-ray data—such as those produced by polychromatic sources subject to scatter and detector flaws—the method offers a pathway to eliminate distortions. Simulation experiments indicate that the TV approach is substantially more effective than both the standard algebraic reconstruction technique (ART) and filtered back-projection (FBP) in such scenarios.

This paper introduces an innovative framework for the semi-supervised learning of automatic speech recognition (ASR) in a cross-lingual context. The approach leverages an unsupervised semi-supervised training technique that merges CycleGAN with inter-domain losses. CycleGAN enables the shared exploitation of a target domain's limited labeled data alongside the target domain's unlabeled data, resulting in improved data utilization. Furthermore, incorporating inter-domain losses facilitates better alignment of decision boundaries in the specific domain, enhancing the model's generalization capabilities. Experiments conducted on the CrossLingual Speech Contexts (CrossLiSCon) dataset, which covers English and Japanese interactions in a car driving scenario using the Hugging Face assistant system, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to other methods. The findings highlight the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing ASR capabilities under low-data constraints within semi-supervised settings.

Active inference serves as a foundational model for understanding how living entities perceive and interact with their surroundings. It posits that its core objective is to reduce surprise by guiding agents to act upon environments conducive to their survival. Although compelling, implementing this theory in its original form proves challenging due to its broad scope; consequently, researchers have developed a variety of constrained versions to render the framework tractable. This paper investigates a specific adaptation of this formulation applied to a multi-armed bandit scenario. Utilizing a state-space model, this approach approximates the active inference objective function through factorized minimum entropy (FEMS), which is then solved via reinforcement learning. The validity of this proposed approach is demonstrated by empirical results that outperform other leading approximate methods across several key metrics. Furthermore, an additional innovation is the introduction of a novel approach to address the computational complexity inherent in estimating the state transition model within such frameworks, thereby enhancing its feasibility for practical application.

This study examines numerically the dynamics of a binary mixture containing dimers and monomers to detect instabilities and potential pattern formation. The system is modeled as a conservative non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation, naturally leading to two distinct non-linear conservation laws. The first law accounts for the separate mass conservations of dimers and mixed dimers-monomers, giving the model its dual structure. Our examination of long-time behavior indicates that the model exhibits multiple steady states and patterns that evolve over time. The equilibrium profile is non-uniform and asymmetric; the system separates into three phases: a region of only dimers, a region of only monomers, and an intermediate domain where both coexist. The composition within this mixed zone is governed by thermodynamic constraints and is further influenced by the initial conditions. Theoretical work has previously established that long-time behaviors in thermodynamic two-phase systems typically involve pattern formation. The underlying cause for the observed pattern formation is identified as a diffusion phenomenon known as the Soret effect. Consequently, our findings are consistent with established theoretical frameworks for conservative non-local Cahn-Hilliard equations.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) constitutes a highly complex task involving multi-aspect generation that requires a deep comprehension of the prompt along with the ability to formulate an appropriate response. Although recent advancements demonstrate that deep learning models have largely overtaken traditional methods in AES research, their capacity to effectively evaluate long-term dependencies remains insufficiently assessed by the community. To address this gap, our study focuses on enhancing the interpretability of the deep learning model by integrating attention mechanisms. Specifically, we employ a specialized Attention-based Recurrent Neural Network (ARNN) architecture, which enables a granular analysis of the attention distribution within hidden states. These insights provide crucial interpretability regarding how the model processes sequences across extended ranges. Our experiments confirm that incorporating these attention-based mechanisms leads to a model that captures long-term dependencies more effectively and produces superior AES outcomes.

A primary obstacle in adapting domain-specific pedestrian detection lies in the presence of unknown objects, a factor that significantly compromises precision. While prior studies have attempted to mitigate these unknowns during domain adaptation, they fail to distinguish between them effectively, largely because they rely on features extracted from fully supervised, single-domain datasets. In contrast, this work addresses unknown object detection in an unsupervised domain-adaptive setting by introducing a novel method to measure the disparity between foreground and background object features specifically within the target domain. By employing a carefully selected network architecture and a dedicated training strategy, the system calculates domain differences at the object level to model foreground-background distinctions more robustly. Evaluations across three widely recognized benchmarks demonstrate that the system substantially improves detection results for unknown objects.

Consumer music tracks recorded by personal devices often suffer from severe degradation due to the inherent limitations of mass-market audio hardware, resulting in significant distortions such as noise, reverberation, and frequency warbling. Although research exists regarding the recovery of these compromised signals, current solutions are restricted by the fact that the original source material is usually unavailable; this is because standard audio tools are a product of a one-to-many process, meaning multiple potential versions of a song can be captured. This study introduces a novel framework designed to resolve this constraint. Our approach assumes that multiple versions of a specific piece of music are accessible within a dataset and proposes a system capable of identifying the optimal single version to minimize auditory distortion. This selection is achieved by evaluating each candidate against a trained, pre-existing neural audio quality estimator.

Although previous research has extensively examined the sensorimotor origins of toy throwing errors made by primates and the impact of these errors on target acquisition, the role of throwing precision in generating these deviations remains largely overlooked. This study introduces a new experimental paradigm in which over-arched throws performed by Rhesus macaques (*Macaca mulatta*) are analyzed using a virtual target system, allowing for the precise measurement of throwing inaccuracy. The results demonstrate that both macaques and human subjects exhibit similar over-armed throwing mechanics and are prone to identical errors. However, the magnitude of error detected in target landing positions varies depending on the timing of the point of release. This finding, coupled with the observation that the macaques consistently land targets, underscores the significance of precision timing and highlights the value of utilizing points of error that align with real-world scenarios. Ultimately, throwing imprecision emerges as a critical factor in understanding the broader evolution of primate projectile-throwing abilities.

We demonstrate a trained, compact MT system that employs a backpropagated neural network with a constitutive algorithm for decoding. Results indicate that these models achieve better translation quality compared to traditional word-by-word approaches while consuming significantly less memory. We also assess two tree-based decoding algorithms and compare them against each other and baseline models. We found that a hierarchy-based model using a constitutive algorithm not only outperforms a word-by-word model in terms of quality but also offers a more efficient decoding process with a shallower search depth. Quantum machine learning (QML) holds significant promise for its ability to process complex data, though its data-driven nature often results in overfitting of small training sets, leading to poor generalization on new inputs. While generalization error can be quantified using the quantum state's variance, estimating this metric requires randomized measurements, which are computationally costly for systems with many qubits. To overcome this, we introduce a novel efficient scheme called "depth-modulated randomized measurement" (DMRM). Unlike previous approaches, DDMR adapts the quantum circuit depth at each step of the measurement, allowing the recovery of generalization-error-state information without the need for deep circuits. Furthermore, we demonstrate the classical simulability of both deep and shallow aspects of this process. Empirical results on generalization errors across randomly chosen training and test datasets show that the simulated outcomes using DDMRU closely match full state reconstructions obtained under ideal noise-free conditions as well as realistic device noise. Finally, both simulations and experiments confirm rapid convergence of the error when data is preprocessed, and these findings hold true across shallow and deeper measurement protocols.

In this study, we establish, under broad assumptions, a connection between the reflection coefficient derived from complex geometric optics waves and Axial S-matrix elements via the LS-algorithm. Specifically, when treated as a function of wave number, the reflection coefficient serves as the Fourier Transform of the target function's real-space representation. Furthermore, this relationship is demonstrated to hold across various families of exact axially symmetric potential scattering solutions.

Transforming text is an emerging and crucial area within Natural Language Processing (NLP) that encompasses tasks such as paraphrasing, translation, and audio-to-text transcription. This study evaluates existing text transformation tools through the concept of "sibylvariance"—defined as randomness in the output that even expert predictors fail to detect. By measuring both human and automated model ability to identify these outputs, we assess their reliability for practical applications. Consequently, the paper proposes a human algorithm capable of distinguishing various text transformation methods, assisted by models trained on these tasks to evaluate and classify the approach used on unclassified inputs.

Meta-learning has emerged as a fundamental area of machine learning, focusing on learning meta-features representing task-specific parameters to facilitate rapid task adaptation. A critical methodology within meta-learning is representation learning, which involves modeling these meta-features in an interpretable format to enable efficient generalization across new tasks. While recent advances have predominantly centered on linear models as interpretable bases, they often fail to capture meaningful representations for complex tasks. This work introduces interpretable sparse support vector machines (IS-SVM) as another task-specific basis, offering superior potential for understanding complex structures. We establish SVM as the optimal choice for interpretable meta-features and derive IS-SVM as its primary model. To effectively learn this representation, an algorithm is developed to optimize the feature space, sparsity constraints, and feature weights jointly. Furthermore, an interpretable generalization strategy is proposed to leverage shared interpretations from previously seen tasks to enhance performance on new ones. The proposed framework, tested within a feature selection context of the 10-fold cross-validation setup on seven standard benchmark datasets, demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy, speed, and computational efficiency compared to current state-of-the-art approaches.

Although state-of-the-art machine translation (MT) systems typically require extensive labeled training data, they often suffer from high memory usage and delayed inference speeds due to large model architectures. While knowledge distillation has been established as a method to resolve the MT challenges of low data availability and high computational demands, our work specifically addresses this approach within neural bigram translation frameworks. Specifically, our findings indicate that distilling large-scale neural machine translation models can serve as a highly effective means of enhancing MT output for data-constrained language pairs.

The primary challenge in developing a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) for a semantic segmentation task in medical imaging is gathering a substantial dataset of chest X-rays (CXRs) annotated with both the disease status and the precise locations of various organs and pathologies. This paper addresses data scarcity by leveraging transfer learning to train a U-Net architecture on a limited subset of CXRs while exploring various augmentation methods to enhance these datasets for better model performance. We evaluated our trained U-Net using two augmentation techniques: a) linear data augmentation and ground truth warping combined with b) non-linear data augmentation using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate additional data samples and corresponding masks. Our findings indicate that linear augmentation is the superior approach, significantly improving model metrics compared to the baseline model trained on minimal data alone. Furthermore, this method reduces the demand for annotated data by up to 50% to achieve equivalent performance gains.

To address this, we present CGCM, a clustering-based framework that separates caption elements and groups them by style to a auto-encoding caption. Empirical results demonstrate that CGCM requires no training yet significantly enhances joint captioning and stylization, as shown by the need for no retraining.

The capacity to explain causality is essential for defining damage and assigning accountability. For autonomous systems, however, the complexity of these systems often obscures the causal links between specific causes and their effects. Our research examines the implications for defining "harm" by integrating a ethical framework for accountability with recent advancements in probabilistic causal models. Our findings show that this synthesized ethical and technical approach yields significant insights into determining harm. Specifically, we identify diverse ways to define "harm" based on actual damage outcomes, potential risks to others, and both positive and negative consequences arising from a system's actions. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural study to simultaneously address causal models and ethical frameworks in defining AI system harm.

This study presents an open-source library named "Tunzai," which integrates popular deep learning tools like TensorFlow and PyTorch with the Apache Spark framework to enable efficient, scalable distributed execution. Tunzai currently offers a comprehensive suite of features, including distributed neural network training for backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent within various network architectures such as feedforward networks, CNNs, and RNNs. Furthermore, the library facilitates resource optimization by dynamically allocating tasks across nodes based on their availability and adjusting execution duration. To support community expansion, Tunzai provides a modular, user-friendly interface that allows seamless integration of additional deep learning components. We are actively seeking feedback from the open-source and AI research communities, and Python bindings have been generated for Java users via Py4J to encourage Java-based contributions.

Speech Translation (ST) involves converting spoken source utterances into written target text. Despite significant advancements in multi-task pre-training, the primary obstacle to achieving zero-shot ST lies in the substantial linguistic disparity between source and target languages, causing models to struggle with accurate translation due to the significant modality mismatch between speech source and text target. Addressing this, we introduce Audio Speech Translation (A2T), an integrated speech-to-speech translation framework capable of handling both speech-to-text and text-to-speech translation within a unified end-to-end mapping architecture using audio inputs and audio outputs. We also present the A2T-X dataset and conduct rigorous zero-shot A2T experiments. The evaluation results indicate that our method can translate bidirectionalally in zero-shot ST tasks by aligning both modality of source and target to audio signals.
